title: FW: 03/03/26: Wie Sparkassen-Berater die "Selbstentscheider" bearbeiten sollen
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Tuesday, 3 March 2026 06:19:41 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 03/03/26: Wie Sparkassen-Berater die "Selbstentscheider" bearbeiten sollen Außerdem: Alle Fintech-News aus Februar, Deutsche Vontobel-Assets erodieren [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/a2a70373-74bb-bbe1-0f2d-9bdec313eccd.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=b5d15508f6&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Was ein Sparkassen-Berater tun soll, wenn er einen "Selbstentscheider" trifft In der Welt der Sparkassen kommen digitale Selbstentscheider bislang nicht vor. So war beispielsweise in einem Handout zur Bilanz-PK der westfälischen Sparkassen letzte Woche von "sogenannten [sic!] digitalen Selbstentscheidern" die Rede. Als ginge es um "sogenannte Außerirdische", Wesen, von denen man zwar immer mal wieder hört, an deren realer Existenz man allerdings berechtigte Zweifel hegt. Das Problem ist nun allerdings, dass es die digitalen Selbstentscheider wirklich gibt, millionenfach sogar, Menschen, die Aktien oder Sparpläne kaufen, ohne zuvor einen Berater konsultiert zu haben  und denen es in vielen Fällen sogar egal ist, ob bei dem Anbieter, über den sie ihre Aktien oder Sparpläne beziehen, im Zweifel jemand ans Telefon geht. So langsam dämmert den Sparkassen: Wenn wir wollen, dass zumindest einige von diesen vielen, vielen oftmals jungen Kunden irgendwann bei uns landen statt bei Trade Republic, Scalable Capital, der DKB oder der ING Diba  dann müssen wir irgendwas tun. Und darum soll nun also "S-Neo" gelauncht werden, der Neobroker der Sparkassen, ein Anbieter für eine Klientel, "die ohne Beratung mit Wertpapieren handeln möchte" und für die "der Kaufvorgang digital, schnell, unkompliziert und möglichst kostengünstig vonstattengehen" soll, wie es bei besagten westfälischen Sparkassen hieß (siehe unsere Meldung hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=cb1bd1384b&e=8f69674dd2>). Alles klar also? Naja, nicht ganz. Denn den Selbstentscheider einfach Selbstentscheider sein lassen  das wollen die Sparkassen laut internen Plänen dann offenbar doch nicht. Bitte sehr: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c6567103f9&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/ef7f4876-6dc3-02d4-af10-203a3a074d76.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ae390a3ffd&e=8f69674dd2> Altersvorsorgedepot-as-a-Service: investify TECH unterstützt bei schneller Umsetzung. Die Altersvorsorgereform bietet ein enormes Geschäftspotenzial. Bei der Umsetzung stoßen Legacy-Systeme oft an ihre Grenzen. investify TECH wird zusammen mit Depotbanken und Asset Managern eine White-Label-Lösung für Banken, Versicherungen, Pools u.a. bieten: schnell, einfach und kostengünstig. Infos hier.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=343cf2dcbd&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Mmhhh, die Banken sollen jeden Blogpost zur KI fürchten  aber keinen Krieg??? Als der "Citrini Report" (benannt nach der Analyse-Firma Citrini, die ihn veröffentlicht hatte) Anfang letzter Woche kurzzeitig die Kurse von Tech- und Payment-Aktien absacken ließ, da kommentierte die "Financial Times" mit hübscher Süffisanz: "The Citrini fuss exposes a market looking for an excuse to fall." Ohne zu sehr ins Detail gehen zu wollen: Die Analysten von Citrini hatten die in den letzten Wochen sehr angesagte Erzählung bedient, wonach der Einsatz künstlicher Intelligenz dermaßen viele Menschen den Job kosten wird, dass mangels Nachfrage die Wirtschaft zusammenbricht (siehe Mitte Februar auch schon > Ist da draußen ein KI-Booster im Anmarsch, der den Banken so richtig weh tut?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=90f580e811&e=8f69674dd2>). Hinzu kamen ein paar Anmerkungen über KI-gestützte Bezahlmittel, was erklärt, warum die Aktien von Visa und Mastercard besonders unter Druck gerieten. Nach ein paar Stunden freilich war der Ausverkauf vorüber, und die Kurse erholten sich wieder. Zurück blieb die Erkenntnis, dass es die KI-Narrative sind, die aktuell die Börsen steigen oder eben bisweilen auch schockhaft fallen lassen ... ... Wenn die USA und Israel dagegen den Iran angreifen, wenn das Regime in Teheran im Gegenzug die Golfstaaten beschießt, wenn im Nahen Osten also ein regionaler Flächenbrand mit potenziell beträchtlichen Folgen für den Welthandel droht und man naiverweise ein Wochenende lang glaubt, dass das doch jetzt tatsächlich mal eine excuse to fall sein sollte  dann tut sich montags an den Märkten kaum etwas. So eröffnete der Dax gestern mit einem angesichts der Umstände fast lächerlich anmutenden Minus von 1,6% (um später bei minus 2,4% zu schließen). Die Deutsche Bank (3,4% auf 29,25 Euro) und die Commerzbank (3,9% auf 33,29 Euro) gaben zwar etwas deutlicher nach  aber keineswegs dramatisch. Kann es unseren Banken und Sparkassen (jenseits der gebotenen politischen Anteilnahme) also mehr oder weniger egal sein, ob da draußen die Welt brennt oder nicht? Nein, natürlich wäre diese Annahme naiv. Das Ausmaß an Unsicherheit ist riesig da draußen. Und wenn man's schon nicht in den Makrodaten sieht, dann ja vielleicht wenigstens auf der Mikroebene. [Sifted_Daily] [Author-TomM] by Tom Matsuda Good morning Luca, In the past two years covering fintech, I’ve slowly seen the sector encroach into popular culture. Fintech sponsors at music festivals are now commonplace, neobank advertising campaigns regularly run across TV and YouTube and celebrity brand partnerships - such as Revolut’s promotion with singer Charli XCX - are becoming increasingly more popular. But fintech’s biggest pop culture moment thus far can be seen in the latest season of the hit HBO show Industry. Where earlier installments of Industry centred on young professionals at an investment bank, season four focuses on Tender, a fintech which started out as a payments processor for grey-market sectors - adult entertainment, porn and gambling - but is now pivoting to become a bank. The show adeptly portrays some of the deep-rooted issues - albeit with dramatic licence - lurking beneath the shiny neon veneer of the fintech industry. Nepotism, fraud and workplaces bereft of personal boundaries take centre stage in the show. There are also boardroom tussles that lead to the ousting of a cofounder, politicians publicly trumpeting fintech innovation and journalists working in parallel with short sellers to investigate Tender’s dodgy dealings. But how realistic is Industry’s depiction of European fintech? With the help of industry sources, I deep dived into what the latest series gets right - and wrong - about the sector. Here’s what I found out. The selloff in software has raised existential concerns for the industry and the future of SaaS players amid the innovations and advancements in AI. While the impact of AI on the software sector is undeniable, to paraphrase Mark Twain, reports of its demise are greatly exaggerated. Software is the DNA powering our world - cars, appliances, communication, collaboration, robotics, and so much more. And while AI can automate and optimize rote and rudimentary functions, true systems of record which house proprietary and confidential data cannot be readily replaced or populated onto open instances of LLMs that lack enterprise grade security, governance and guardrails. Yes, software is under attack, but do not count it out just yet. People are worried about private credit liquidity The basic situation is that people work for about 40 years, during which they earn more money than they spend, and then they retire and dont work for about 30 years, during which they spend more money than they earn. [1] Thats a very broad statement, you could quibble with the numbers, and it is certainly not true of everyone: Some people retire early, some retire late, some die young, some live a long time, etc. [2] But as a rough statistical average, most people get some decades of saving in the workforce and then some decades of spending in retirement. At that rough statistical level, you could model out how much the people need to save in the first 40 years to be able to afford their lifestyle in the next 30 years. The model is of the form if you invest X% of your income during your working years, and your investments return Y% per. year, then in retirement you can draw down Z% of your investments each year to continue to live a similar lifestyle, something like that. If you do this in your own life, and calibrate the model exactly right, and all of your assumptions work out, then you will maintain a consistent lifestyle for the whole 70-year period and run out of money on the day that you die. But almost nobody will actually achieve that, or probably even want to. Some people will save more or less, some people will get higher or lower investment returns, some people will live longer or shorter than expected, etc. Also, of course, lots of people wont calibrate the model exactly right, or model this out at all, or save money. So a lot of people will die with money left over, and a lot of other people will run out of money too soon. But at a level of statistical aggregates, its easier to get things right: Some people will have too much, some people will have too little, but they will cancel each other out and there will be enough money in aggregate. In other words, this problem is one that is natural to address with risk pooling: If everyone saves the same share of their income in the same pot, they can all replace the same share of their working income during retirement, and people who for whatever accidental reason have too much will subsidize the people who for whatever accidental reason have too little. This is of course the theory behind defined-benefit pension funds; it is also loosely speaking the theory behind Social Security in the US. Thats the other thing that private means: They dont trade continuously in public markets. If you are investing in OpenAI equity or data-center loans, you cant easily get your money back tomorrow, so you dont want your own investors to ask for their money back tomorrow. If all your investors ask for their money back, you will have to sell those data-center loans in an opaque and restricted market, and youll probably get a bad price. But when you sell private investments to thousands of individual investors, they dont have the actuarial risk pooling that a pension fund has. Some of them are 45 years old, dont plan to retire for 20 years, have plenty of money and really should be able to lock some of it up for seven years  but are they sure? What if they have a medical emergency tomorrow and need their money back? The individual retirement savers have to manage their own risks, so they want liquidity; they dont want to lock up their money the way a big pooled institutional investor would. And so if you sell private investments to thousands of individual investors, you have to make them some promise like you can get your money back whenever you want. Or perhaps you make a promise like you can get some of your money back sometimes, but the investors hear I can get my money back whenever I want. As an actuarial matter this isnt that bad, because after all you are doing some pooling: If you raise money from 10,000 individual retirement savers, most of them wont need their money back for 20 years, so you can safely invest 95% of it in long-term private investments and keep 5% to meet a few withdrawal requests. In fact a lot of retail-oriented private-market funds offer liquidity in a form like we will let people withdraw money every quarter, but capped at 5% of the funds assets each quarter. Should be fine for most peoples needs. But the problem is not some of my investors have medical emergencies and need their money back. The problem is there are bad headlines about private credit and all of my investors want their money back. If you offer your retail investors liquidity, they will use it, in a correlated way and at the worst time: not when they need the money for retirement, but when they see some bad news on television and panic. If you let them all take their money out at once, then you have a run on the bank, you have to sell your private assets, the whole point of those assets is that you cant sell them quickly or efficiently, the market is nervous anyway, and so your investors lose money. If you dont let them all take their money out at once, then you have a marketing problem: They all want liquidity, and if you cant give it to them then they will go back to their low-cost index funds and never invest in private markets again. What you want, in other words, is a pension fund for a client. What you want is one big client who pools the funds of a bunch of retirement savers, locks up their money, tells them dont you worry about this but in 20 years, when you retire, youll have income, and then is able to make its own investment decisions, take long-term risk and earn a liquidity premium. Taking money directly from individual investors creates liquidity risk, but taking money from individual investors through annuity providers mitigates that risk. Stake/Drake People like to gamble on the results of random number generators. Usually they dont like to bet on things that are explicitly random number generators; usually it is more appealing if things are dressed up a bit. title: Businessweek Live at Bloomberg Invest | Bloomberg Businessweek Daily 3/03/2026
content: On today's episode of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily, Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec discuss a risk-off move gripping markets to start Tuesday as investors digest Iran war headwinds. Brookfield Asset Management CEO Connor Teskey weighs in from Bloomberg Invest, and also discusses the state of private credit. Then, Bloomberg's Eric Weiner recaps today's price action as stocks and bonds sink and oil rallies. Plus, NYSE President Lynn Martin weighs in on the IPO backdrop as candidates look to get deals done amid geopolitical uncertainty. Next, MongoDB CEO CJ Desai on the company's recent earnings and investor worries as the stock sinks as far as 20% Tuesday. Finally, Ariel Investments Founder & CEO John Rogers on value investing and the US consumer. (Source: Bloomberg)

Some European VCs tell Sifted the new conflict in the Middle East has exposed a worrying technological gap between Europe and other nations like the US and Iran. “All bets are off for European defence after seeing Shahed drones being intercepted above the cityscape of Dubai,” says Jack Wang, a partner at German venture capital firm Project A, which has backed drone startups including Quantum Systems and Stark. “Iran, Israel and the US are using military technology that are still R&D-ing Series A startups in Europe.” It all underscores the “urgency” for Europe to bolster its defence capabilities and technologies, adds Hugo Jammes, managing partner of defence-focused fund EDT Ventures and a former investor at the UK’s National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF) - something defence VCs are clearly keen to see for their own portfolios, too. title: FW: 04/03/26: DSGV wackelt bei Kleinbanken-Regime, Youlend macht Berlin zum EU-Hub
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Wednesday, 4 March 2026 06:15:19 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 04/03/26: DSGV wackelt bei Kleinbanken-Regime, Youlend macht Berlin zum EU-Hub Außerdem: Raisin launcht in Italien, DZ-Bank-Analyse, Wero startet E-Com in Belgien [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/90a1d9cf-34b8-0542-edab-a179802d3e8c.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=d76244bddf&e=8f69674dd2> DZ Bank pulverisiert Ergebnisrekord  doch nur 27% kommen aus dem Bankgeschäft Glaubt man Cornelius Riese, dem Chef der DZ Bank, dann verfügt sein Haus über ein natürliches Ergebnisniveau irgendwo zwischen 2 Mrd. und 3 Mrd. Euro (bis 2024 sprach Riese von 2,02,5 Mrd. Euro, seitdem von 2,53,0 Mrd. Euro). Ironischerweise ist es aber so, dass das tatsächliche Ergebnis irgendwie nie dem natürlichen Niveau entspricht. Entweder, die DZ Bank landet oberhalb von 3 Mrd. Euro (2021, 2023, 2024). Oder sie landet unterhalb von 2 Mrd. Euro (2020, 2022). Aber sie landet nie mittendrin. Wie ein Elfmeterschütze, der mal rechts vorbeischießt und mal links, aber der partout nicht das gut sieben Meter breite Tor treffen will. Das alles liegt nun wiederum daran, dass die DZ Bank unter ihrem Dach einen Versicherer beherbergt, dessen Ergebnisse aus Gründen, die wir nicht verstehen, aber als Banken-Newsletter auch nicht verstehen müssen ("versicherungstechnisch"), wie ein Fähnlein im Sturm flattern. Mal macht die R+V kaum Gewinn (2020). Mal schreibt sie sogar Verlust (2022). Und mal (genauer: 2025) macht sie dermaßen viel Gewinn, dass in der Ableitung die DZ Bank dermaßen viel Gewinn macht, dass in der zweiten Ableitung eine große Wirtschaftszeitung gestern vermeldete, die DZ Bank habe im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr sogar mehr Gewinn gemacht als die Commerzbank (merke: Wenn ein Apfel richtig, richtig dick ist, dann ist er mitunter sogar dicker, als eine Birne hoch ist). Oder anders gesagt: Die DZ Bank hat bei ihrer gestrigen Bilanz-PK also einen Fabelrekordgewinn in Höhe von surrealen 4,3 Mrd. Euro präsentiert. Was aber nicht unbedingt etwas über ihre aktuelle Performance aussagt. Hier die Ergebnisse in der Einzel-Analyse: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=26d5bfaf0f&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/fddbd541-e814-7619-6a08-55f825c65ca5.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=76492befe1&e=8f69674dd2> Wachstum scheitert nicht an Marktchancen, sondern an Prozessen. Mit Sinpex wird KYB zum skalierbaren Enabler statt zum Bottleneck. Schnellere Aktivierung, geringere operative Kosten und vollständige Audit-Sicherheit  auch bei steigenden Volumina und neuen regulatorischen Anforderungen. So bleibt Compliance unter Kontrolle, während Ihr Geschäft weiter wächst. Erfahren Sie mehr.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=00b1718712&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Mit einem Tag Verspätung brechen die Aktien von DBK und Coba doch noch ein: Nachdem Bankinvestoren am Montag noch erstaunlich abgebrüht auf die Ereignisse in Nahost reagiert hatten (siehe > Unsere Banken sollen jeden Blogpost zur KI fürchten  aber keinen Krieg???<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=12fcf05866&e=8f69674dd2>), sind die Kurse am Dienstag nun doch deutlich abgesackt. So verlor die Deutsche-Bank-Aktie satte 4,3% auf 27,99 Euro  der tiefste Stand seit Juli , für die Commerzbank ging es um 4,9% auf nur noch 31,66 Euro runter. Freilich waren die beiden größten deutschen Geldinstitute damit keine Ausnahme. So gab der Euro Stoxx Banks um 4,5% nach, die Unicredit büßte 4,6% auf 66,92 Euro ein ... ... Eine interessante Facette ist dabei, dass der Aktienkurs der Unicredit, seit die Italiener am 9. Februar ihre überaus ambitionierte neue Strategie<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ad21705fbf&e=8f69674dd2> präsentierten, deutlich stärker gelitten hat als der europäische Bankenmarkt insgesamt. Seit dem an jenem Tag erreichten Höchstkurs hat die Unicredit-Aktie inzwischen 15% verloren, während das Kursminus der Commerzbank im gleichen Zeitraum lediglich 10% beträgt. Für ein etwaiges Übernahmeangebot (die Unicredit dürfte hierzu neuerdings ja auch Aktien als Akquisewährung einsetzen) nicht die allergünstigste Entwicklung. Blog Exklusiv: Sparkassen deuten spektakuläre Wende beim Kleinbanken-Regime an. Bislang unterstützte der DSGV (ebenso wie der BVR) die Leverage-Ratio-basierten Pläne der Bafin. Doch nun  zeichnet sich nach Informationen von Finanz-Szene ein bemerkenswerter Positionswechsel ab. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=2397c5e833&e=8f69674dd2> News * Trotz des surrealen Rekordgewinns (siehe oben) bleibt die DZ Bank in puncto Dividende knausrig. Die örtlichen Volks- und Raiffeisenbanken sollen lediglich eine unveränderte Ausschüttung von 25 Cent je Aktie erhalten  das entspricht hochgerechnet gerade mal 18% des Nettogewinns. * Bei der Postbank ist es in den letzten Tagen zu IT-bedingten Problemen bei der Ausführung von Daueraufträgen gekommen. Dabei wurden für den 1. März geplante Zahlungen entweder gar nicht gebucht oder im Nachgang sofort wieder dem Absenderkonto gutgeschrieben. Inzwischen sei das Problem behoben, heißt es auf Anfrage. * Die NordLB soll nach dem Willen der niedersächsischen Sparkassen (die 36% der Anteile halten) auch in diesem Jahr auf eine Dividendenzahlung verzichten. "Meine persönliche Meinung ist, dass das Eigenkapital lieber in der Bank bleiben sollte", sagte Verbandschef Cord Bockhop. Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/6b674de9-d161-489b-7c26-7132b04cc1c8.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=73aae94b02&e=8f69674dd2> Mit Baader Trading können Sie handeln, solange die News aus aller Welt aktuell sind. Kurz Der Berliner Einlagen-Broker Raisin vermeldet seinen Marktstart in Italien (wobei er dort unserer Erinnerung nach mittels einer Kooperation mit der Banca Sella vor ein paar Jahren schon mal angetreten war) +++ Die EPI-Wallet Wero rollt ihre E-Commerce-Lösung jetzt auch in Belgien aus  erste Händler seien bereits live, hieß es gestern +++ Das britische Fintech Youlend (hierzulande als Finanzierungspartner von Amazon bekannt<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=47a7c6f31a&e=8f69674dd2>) will seine Berliner Niederlassung zum neuen EU-Hub mit rund 70 Mitarbeitern ausbauen (Finance Fwd<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=28bcbb7ae6&e=8f69674dd2>) Ticker * Die gestern vorgestellten Zahlen der hessisch-thüringischen und niedersächsischen Sparkassen bestätigen den Gesamteindruck der bisherigen Bilanzsaison. title: Bloomberg Invest: AI, Credit, and Risk | Open Interest 3/4/2026
content: Get a jump start on the US trading day with Matt Miller and Dani Burger on "Bloomberg Open Interest." It’s day two of Bloomberg Open Interest on the road at the Bloomberg Invest Conference — where the power players shaping the future of money take center stage. Today, the biggest investors in private capital reveal where the smart money is really moving in the AI boom. Julie Solomon of Ares on the new economy land grab. Scott Kapnick of HPS on whether private credit can withstand a higher-for-longer world. Marsh CEO John Doyle talks about how global insurers price war risk as conflict in the Middle East escalates. Bruce Richards of Marathon Asset Management warns leveraged software default rates could hit 15%. Is software the next energy-style blowup? And State Street’s Yie-Hsin Hung on how institutional investors are positioning as geopolitical turmoil roils markets. (Source: Bloomberg)

BCRED Lets say that you work in private credit and you think that private credit is great. Oh, sure, youve seen all the headlines; you know people are worried about SaaSpocalypses<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/lIwFb8VcKVZXX_761jd3n95xImyS539ZfU29TLDPbfVVbwS8m3GMHXyUpNZWlcWd8Pp4MG3LJ9iTWiBYW2zNbdRdRvYDGyOy340OGcR8ttJm7zjoESsQN6IiIkH36T06859IcQ2KcSaHSsX8MXXW_qyhV_IY5WIfeSabp7RTsRnctgUqsL5G1o4uzfP5PUfb0WZloMy4p_ZBIMM24oxhYPYON412wVrfpaEP-C2RDK7jXLdwLLmVuYxmjr2tMvK0wzJGyAF7Z70WHQ6-NmJvrdv6HcdcI5zxBMgveBdJ7hOV8QAC_K3_I4RpoSxVdUpKFoi3Kulz7F_FYgl3TZe_sM1g7-xhZ1qSBuaW-uOJyUqmtAPUVv-OCz9-kw/rh_C9PnKmR1o_TGt-RpQ_hN5EXV0F3qU/18> and cockroaches<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/ykQcfaySqwScoe9M5lM1lnY0RKf6E3YvSVKM6FI8SPHrIyrnBg2kdi2zvV3z9O3cABLtA0zCr0hhU9GZoIaRAge2sucSi8D7pHaoMlggD3R_b94Psi0wCxew1Xu0Kap20Ai9-aTGHdnauzVYc_hwIUZimiWZ_BJMhI395XgvGyeAVnplO0BTuSEqPD07pHP8Ees2_M4jmFjz81TCegLHexZbYc7ZHj6SdYZJAqLhuhnVNMVeS9k9NUvYliBuP-zWkSpJUGAR-xmG8YWnywxKtDUvOMmbvyNzpr3uouVyuoShVgWbkZRjHQGLmzQ-wJO3cxz8JzibV05GKX1LKvlNapkdZY0GDGvcWdpX0FMdix0SVAdL1zF2S1B7OA/4nzP7gJU4590IFz_q0NZ_rbkBVsL4SVs/18> and so forth. You just think theyre wrong. You did the deals, you know the credits, and you think that all of these loans are going to work out great and pay back par. How should you trade that thesis? The obvious intuitive answer is something like: If people are panicking and want to sell their shares of private credit funds for 80 cents on the dollar, and you think theyre worth 100 cents on the dollar, you should buy them at 80 cents on the dollar. And then youll make 20 cents. Good trade, if youre right. But the details here are a bit tricky. Loosely speaking there are about three sorts of private credit funds: 1. There are what you might call institutional funds, drawdown funds and separately managed accounts for institutional investors. Stereotypically, the investors in these funds arent looking to sell their shares at 80 cents on the dollar: The whole point<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/fH9uxvWpWfxM-gVJVrCM2eeXF3dzMc5jab71QBIB3_2PYXlDQ0rdKqEura4pe_lKFuCVsO4xRfCD5p4zv1Jiz1il8Abd3qub2X5ktng7ACmfcQ2jBfMF8S4kGVUyqn86RMPKEdC7z6EocE6tWa_Pbbpm51jqHqxeCGKC4LHLP4hNSFp1IndNJV38oVTdeyaZFMv0Ea_N5bBNKGBhfiEZnMhJ5lmaQpOcdLkikQAYkE1-iFX7J2GRSeJ2nghYK98kFYUrjXax499hnbrWb-NVh_e-Jx3Fcywm0N0p_KTWsZsxu0Ympx5uN7CEGUTKlV1tcTiehz5r00sbIHDWSaFNO2r6pQ6G8Z7LqEW72HCCkc4j0mG87ysgc4eECA/HNzizWEIEHJspnR7kJwDdNkmNGldUYcc/18> of those funds is that the investors money is locked up for some pre-set period, and the whole point<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/71iVwqyT_2SEEE3V4FcFmXsHeX5U8jyjWjJ4f1wzZRX6CW-2L93jdBi-rEmoBECjymCCeVHlzRycgjF2YgDsmTjya3FwDjnFZH9FCL7f1KMLnqXlKwvycw4kAL2zkWhHtq6EmpakijGWbJ5couqlCsL-CcTh_7bIBJS1v4RmfCLIc8N2b3dfxvLGAfAHBBQG9095jU7FdRpsuE0UZM9U2q1WHm4YmQVQtRhXdvafd3Iu0ynzQWX1EfJiE63ZfxU5SUJuw1tH1x2jhJdHA6QbC3VRN3jIMtAx8AwZ24bd8_bmN-G3qRAGLqGy6k5zrs3c51Srx9H_7prO3F4xKJbUvEd4-38gz_EjTyv8r7x0fCfpUDkXkC3AcSybQQ/OFsEGs7kMjtNmKf3DkLbE6Q9qlMt_5VD/18> of the investors is that they are institutions who can afford to lock up their money. (In fact there is some secondary trading of private credit fund stakes<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/fhAe3FVPT1z_2NmUe1CKd1tgURaFMr8RnGDAGhbfJsPMmEGs6MSSoPg6bxfT_kfqX3L0KVtirhDK6Y6arg6O1Rkb_k-Jka8Qd0cAcuAt9IArsU--XUik5wuox1vjgXj2Tmvl4x3_k4uc-gmDs61g3N1cKYSu5Jfp_36o-enS5_LYTYos2OBmmiV22m_Xh2JVZHApCF7o7_nTQabol_MHaWhlrj-lk9Y7jZqgd17ToUuVI6pt-V0Fbix4KhA3P66pv_mjmB9320e6JVZ4YVXfJTdR0_4dUxQpbwcnG-MJL1dTnlwNGOOa4X8lq9Y3sMYptTmciKD6u8oZfNKFbhYYQCPCpnNV2rIsRBNw-BlkeHnTMtvwA90vq6Z-Zw/KdgNx8YAvBG1rtW5lsz2HEbd2ImOcW1m/18>, but it still seems pretty nascent<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/LTMbtqHM4M7sgHvFoVR684x1ibLdJCdrKofAxnlq8hmputNtvIYKSdte_qZQPspbJWtWEeo14X3BOz-H2UJVmZiUQW3lzLEG3of0E8t6uKi0yPH9OEixPniIpPOwWrXPsvoXrVMaTHPNxSKUlDEK2ceA7b9oiB6DYKPtoa1UGHaDCYTJTcn1jBoS_PGEup1eOMdT0LSZ4i9PIUxdxmj9gBcD6bUd7PbsTDnyNLwiNWSZ9lzerTzQAsiIFmAlrLUkZ6iqSpSiNlvJpyW1jGc4ZHgm5no_nWppnI44w1-_sh34yFcWFskAviWH015kO9IpxDf59cEG4i8XfSKqsPkPK32jE9gcQSzHaikCKPjmB-k5_23vR4cM5-hb3Eg/jAK0nmQqJhK9ZRzuPL4atoKR1aYWpt9x/18>, and you might have a hard time finding sellers.) Also, these institutions expect their private-assets portfolio to have very low volatility<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/fpENwMCBPP-Qwi4p_j46MKi8o_ZuuhCWPraCgGbNEIUGEDIfH91WSkJyidNhN_FbsGD8fA1cko6cMZ6vI5MMKJny5IfWqN8TN4WP2nYXg6KYdNAKwzGxDdI56QzqVgTKbDJ4IfcMsAqHn0CnOR6sg8lLNf1pFnnaF98ZURQal7DpHEaHQQa43chs0B9U0oXbQ_GQYH-MeQ22fhPjlyjLB9dc8QSbHEC17YtUMz9Tu3i19fJ40Lzy9YbjvoeFl3cpsRy89n9yyIYN54MhmUkU1MiSB8SeqH09sNNqE7qQS1bQ8rYwieIEgOP-oUHI1nFe5IRUKVJLQ7hIBCcibwTxvODkKIjqVmK5DfYELmtTAlZehJ8_QSWj8FhoR6Q/j5etdxM2r0PjrdlTyGzR6tc9MW2TpOGc/18>, so if you called them up and offered to buy at 80 cents on the dollar theyd be offended. So this is not a promising way to do this trade. 2. There are publicly traded business development companies, which are retail-oriented permanent private credit funds that trade on the stock exchange. A bunch of those really are trading at 80 cents on the dollar<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/7BxE0jeuEkhzskl1YwUOkLETh49J0EWlymVPjj7-IpNkN7FVZXnP-dhGN3V_ncuMMIeGTEvYUeB7Ut20CBrZf2KzVqdHg1GnTAQCtJ2UT7kt1DrLo9N1nYmY1u5-UVany-Vbi7FsIqcrBWEypLDejyc8LWWiRap_RFN29o3nz5Yv6h3tXX4YuibnDe_q_k0l5nglBfOftFRPOPyPJGSCCtzzb6iJ5ItYlgSlZm1zxN_eo_zp3FEZ-REC82VkcFBjBWutPwmpsaBjOJj6uIJVw90hb7_SdUwM8WpmSJkcfiBEatCE5SFpKTySreR5lA_eVPHya_LJIxzEz9xqjVrqaTnjw6ptQVb3pgpvSIBjdtSmpQ6Cmm_J34qQmPw/pDTH6qTkMDlXWm8RLG7Zs96b-QyEQ7fc/18>; BlackRock Inc. has one trading below 50. You can just buy them on the stock exchange. This is a straightforward and easy way to do this trade. 3. There are private, unlisted business development companies, retail-oriented private credit funds that are sold by wealth advisers to individual investors and that dont trade on the stock exchange. The investors in those funds generally cant sell their shares, at 80 cents on the dollar or otherwise, because the shares dont trade. Instead, the managers of the funds offer to buy back some of the shares periodically  typically a maximum of 5% per quarter  so that investors who want out can get out. And the managers normally do this at net asset value<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/eBjsMs9C7tYIfm6ZprHAMIALL8gaR6HlXs2yvSVRzGEt09psOkw6fazSaBfGJl1ALkX6VKpQeTOrmxyc8IspwI8HOkOHTbNUFIStvL6AG3lSViVkh-ZjKxI3ViVt8pmwYBVIE0c6BrjHSQLRfmJg1r4CGNB747AQFBNliBXXYFJCknGeY7hS97XedEOFrospDxzQM-UiK1xQPFFGk7kGNov5AyM1PmEseemNOCEU-C_Sw6B8RhLXuDfS8z0VTr0Us4bcsrg2LQ43yIixKDrZpEae6pWfmv2h6e3idiKVk_z3rFLw0Prngt9PF6cF8gCWISf0wAPAajg6dp6M2uhoZXz3Hn7ClvYX1O7NE-zbCCwJiinYedzIDOJDVp8/nM_1UpTvLTXYhmvvO1n-1DwqGfEjau0p/18>: If the loans are all marked at 100 cents on the dollar, then the tender price is 100 cents on the dollar. Most of the bad headlines, these days, are about the third category, the non-traded BDCs, for somewhat intuitive reasons. People who invest in public BDCs that trade at 80 cents on the dollar will naturally be disappointed  they wanted 100 cents on the dollar  but market prices are market prices and you cant really complain. But people who invest in private BDCs have been asking for their money back, and they are worried that they wont get it. We have talked about a Blue Owl Capital Inc. private BDC, called OBDC II, that stopped doing those quarterly 5% redemptions<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/0LLv8vU57ynyMq_W7FhEHN_yMq6lWR0BN52p_jo_PoWHSZjjb65ei5Cyl6Gr-mlR1paK876OE9BYCnxVmbp3uPyktHlMybPpJiwCdBcKY6y4SrxtyDdtj7b1ypmqVAFjMQNYcDVs4HbcQylh3MpR327j0ovn2YikTOSH-4UZ1I8vkByATDRuytbCV7NA1sqWCioYPH0ZTJSZCLs-awaGN72XqegT_PiiIYCP6VvKjJsvwMrHMbB_DTrP1J6mbS9afDFIsq0xrnie2hQXjpYiO-ZdSb0U89qLaPpoafz5g3hGI_-eercPmPM7llZbO5jrKZLph-7YNLWQnLuvj4wEZoa4uasgGMEsRxVwfHA1DGC3uMC-4kTllYNSJ_8/Et37xdI1QY5LHU6wteRbF-uQDLOTuvbn/18>. And now Blackstone Group Inc.s main private BDC, called BCRED, has gotten redemption requests for considerably more than 5% of its money<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/YJo18OUes6440aOMznfrjEDAVXjZut2ZQbZhS59IhpcYX_0ZnbGNak8hW8xE3GomFXiTTBGMLAk-Bjh3tlYL_wm-b5iXxax2sT9rXYhtF9ESxh5byM0vOjqfR1pHUrEDU3kcuXI5iWhNrVxYqqVUmWjMfDCW2tJJiiucqNnwrAfrNdvTpmZXUSA0LsGpfOLuBJ5_rKeDkzVtW9UFYB4nwoCot1-C2kjjCbw8fYaygGN7aLwAmsLntRJIf21gaj9rClgqw29RQOt7va0h1gTArDnklwns12nQrTxwzvvzU8E9Ln--z0J0Lsp5qEETVud2XUk-__f3ow3Qp38rzUA8jFvvK_izgY2okNGz_QVbnSW7JTkXLLfqjWzCnvQ/oRY5bDpxmXYg0EcTrpZjILplxGBOsETm/18>: Blackstone Inc. is allowing investors to redeem a record 7.9% of shares from its flagship private credit fund, the latest sign of unease in an industry thats faced a wave of withdrawals. The firm is meeting the requests, which are equivalent to around $3.8 billion, by increasing the size of a previously announced tender offer to 7% of the funds total shares and by stepping in, alongside employees, to offset the remaining 0.9%, according to a filing and a spokesperson. The fund has around $82 billion of total assets, including leverage, the filing shows. Blackstone didnt have to give all those people their money back, but it did, because not doing so would be a marketing nightmare. If a public BDC trades below net asset value, well, thats life in the public markets. But if a private BDCs investors ask for their money back, and just dont get it, they might panic, and the whole retail-private-credit business model might be in danger. Whole business securitization The basic way that corporate debt works is that a company gets some revenue, and then it pays its necessary expenses, and then it pays its debt out of whats left over, and then if theres money left after that it can spend it on new investments or frivolous expenses or executive pay or stock buybacks or whatever. So if a company has $100 of debt and makes $400 of revenue, it might spend $250 on salaries and rent and utilities and all the other stuff that is absolutely required to keep the lights on and bring in that revenue, and it will have about $150 left over. And it will send $100 of that to its creditors and keep the other $50 for whatever its executives and shareholders want. That is a very fuzzy description, though. Usually the way debt works is that, when a company borrows money, it wont have to pay that money back for several years; it will make interest payments along the way, but those will be much smaller than the principal of the debt. If, during the intervening years, the company mostly squanders its money, then when the debt comes due it wont be able to pay. Everyone understands this, so the debt will probably contain covenants prohibiting the company from squandering the money too egregiously, but this is hard to measure and in fact companies often do go bankrupt and default on their debt. You could imagine formalizing the fuzzy description from my first paragraph. When it wants to borrow money, the company could sit down with its lenders and agree on an explicit flowchart for its revenue: * The first $X of revenue every month goes to pay necessary expenses to operate the business. X is fixed; the creditors and the company agree on what the necessary expenses are and how much they will be. The company doesnt get to change its mind later; it cant decide to get into new business lines and increase the expenses it deems necessary. The necessary expenses are just fixed in advance for the life of the loan. * The next $Y of revenue goes into a box to pay down the debt over time. The creditors dont have to wait seven years to get paid back; the money flows back to them each month. * Anything left over goes to the company for new investments, frivolous expenses etc. This is, in general, kind of a bad way to run a big company, and most companies want more flexibility than this. But for certain sorts of companies with pretty stable revenue and expenses, this can work. For instance, restaurant brand companies  which make steady revenue from franchise fees and have reasonably straightforward management expenses  sometimes do deals like this, which are called whole business securitizations. Just the words whole business securitization sound terrible. The theory of a whole business securitization is that (1) you can borrow money secured by your whole business but (2) that debt is safer  it should get a better credit rating and a lower interest rate  than regular corporate debt would be. Because you fix your expenses and put your revenue in a box, and your lenders buy bonds of that box, they are getting a different, better proposition than just buying bonds of your company. The box has more reliable cash flows and is more protected from your bad business decisions, so it is safer and the debt should cost less. Last year, a record 6% of workers in 401(k) plans administered by Vanguard Group took a hardship withdrawal. That is up from 4.8% in 2024 and a prepandemic average of about 2%, according to Vanguard. The data paint a divergent financial picture of American workers finances. While most are faring well, some are experiencing heightened financial stress, according to Vanguard. Workers have been saving more in 401(k)s, and balances have soared to all-time highs along with rising markets. With more people saving in 401(k)s, retirement accounts are an increasingly important lifeline when financial trouble hits. If the main way you save for retirement is in an account that you manage, with a dollar balance that you can check every day, you might end up spending those dollars before retirement. I should add that it is a bit too simplistic to say that, if a companys executives do something you dont like, you can sue for securities fraud. Your damages, in a securities fraud lawsuit, will be tied to your losses as a shareholder, which means in practice that you can only sue for securities fraud if (1) the company did something you dont like and (2) the stock went down when the thing was revealed. title: FW: 05/03/26: Restwert-Kollaps - deutsche Santander erlebt Fiasko in der Auto-Finanzierung
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Thursday, 5 March 2026 06:19:34 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 05/03/26: Restwert-Kollaps  deutsche Santander erlebt Fiasko in der Auto-Finanzierung Außerdem: Genos funden Amberra mit 100 Mio. , Finoa-Gründer zieht sich zurück [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/90a1d9cf-34b8-0542-edab-a179802d3e8c.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c9f45675cd&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Restwert-Kollaps  deutsche Santander erlebt Fiasko in der Auto-Finanzierung Wer "Autobank" hört, denkt normalerweise an die VW Bank, die BMW Bank oder die Mercedes Bank. Ein riesiger Player in dem Bereich ist allerdings auch die Santander Consumer Bank, bei der es sich zwar nicht um eine Autobank im klassischen Sinne handelt (da sie zu keinem Automobilkonzern gehört)  die dafür allerdings an etlichen Autobanken beteiligt ist und sich stolz den "größten herstellerunabhängigen Kfz-Finanzierer" in Deutschland nennt. Klar, die Connaisseure wissen all das! Historischer Vorläufer der heutigen Santander Consumer Bank war schließlich die Mönchengladbacher CC-Bank, die zwar nicht nur, aber auch in der Absatzfinanzierung für Autohändler tätig war. Ähnliches galt für die Hannoveraner GE Money Bank, welche 2009 in der deutschen Santander aufging. Mitte der 2010er-Jahre startete dann die VCFS Germany GmbH (ein 50:50-Joint Venture zwischen Santander und Volvo)  ungefähr zur gleichen Zeit erfolgte der Einstieg bei der PSA Bank Deutschland (Peugeot/Citroën), wobei dieser 50%-Stake ein paar Jahre später wieder abgestoßen wurde. Dafür allerdings erwarb die Santander im Jahr 2019 die Mehrheit an der Frankfurter Hyundai Capital Bank Europe, über die man sich ein Jahr später (zu einem bemerkenswerten Kaufpreis von 342 Mio. Euro) zusätzlich die Sixt Leasing einverleibte. Und damit nicht genug, ließ man 2023 auch noch die rund 90%-ige Mehrheitsübernahme der MCE Bank GmbH (Flörsheim a. M.) folgen, welche als Finanziererin unter anderem für Mitsubishi und Isuzu auftritt. Um die Sache also abzukürzen: Es ist ein gigantisches Rad, das die Santander Consumer Bank da dreht. Und allem Anschein nach hat es inmitten dieses Portfolios nun einen heftigen Einschlag (und zusätzlich 1-2 kleinere Einschläge) gegeben. Unsere exklusive Recherche: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=80e2fb8dd1&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/fddbd541-e814-7619-6a08-55f825c65ca5.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=48e8b1760a&e=8f69674dd2> Wachstum scheitert nicht an Marktchancen, sondern an Prozessen. Mit Sinpex wird KYB zum skalierbaren Enabler statt zum Bottleneck. Schnellere Aktivierung, geringere operative Kosten und vollständige Audit-Sicherheit  auch bei steigenden Volumina und neuen regulatorischen Anforderungen. So bleibt Compliance unter Kontrolle, während Ihr Geschäft weiter wächst. Erfahren Sie mehr.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e9b3e147ec&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Exklusiv: Amberra hat die 100 Mio. Euro beisammen  diese Volksbanken sind dabei. Wie das bei Verbund-Projekten halt manchmal so ist, ging's auch bei Amberra anfangs etwas rumpelig zu (siehe etwas dieses Stück hier von Ende 2022<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c5431fa7bf&e=8f69674dd2>). Nun allerdings, knapp vier Jahre nach der Ankündigung und rund zwei Jahre nach dem Launch, hat das genossenschaftliche "Venture Studio" das angepeilte Zielvolumen von 100 Mio. Euro für seinen Wagniskapital-Fonds tatsächlich beisammen. Das Kapital dafür komme von insgesamt 180 der rund 650 genossenschaftlichen Primärbanken, erklärte Amberra-CEO Björn Schmuck diese Woche im Gespräch mit Finanz-Szene  wobei insgesamt mehr als die Hälfte der Bilanzsumme der Gruppe repräsentiert sei. Die durchschnittliche Investitionssumme pro Institut liegt also bei rund 550.000 Euro. Zu den beteiligten Banken gehören laut Amberra die Hannoversche Volksbank und die Volksbank Raiffeisenbank Würzburg. Wie Finanz-Szene darüber hinaus aus dem Verbund hört, sollen auch die Berliner Volksbank und die Frankfurter Volksbank Rhein/Main (also die zwei größten deutschen VR-Banken) sowie weitere Metropol-Volksbanken wie die aus Stuttgart und Hamburg am Start sein. [Sifted_Daily] [Author-Anne] by Anne Sraders Good morning Luca, The EU’s new Scaleup Europe Fund has fast become one of VC’s hottest topics. At €5bn, it will be the region’s largest ever funding vehicle - and a major prize for whichever firm wins the rights to run it - prompting intense speculation around the selection process. The fund, set to launch this spring, will back deeptech companies across the region. Applications to oversee the multi-billion euro pot closed last month, and those that have advanced to the next stage of the process will be invited to present in Brussels next week, Sifted reports. title: Brookfield's Connor Teskey on State of Private Credit
Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein on Why He Doesn't Tweet
content: Lloyd Blankfein was CEO of Goldman Sachs for more than a decade, riding the trading boom to the top of the storied investment bank and steering it through the 2008 financial crisis. In his new memoir, Streetwise: Getting To and Through Goldman Sachs, he writes about his journey from public housing in Brooklyn to the pinnacle of Wall Street. So what's he up to now? And how does he see markets and finance today? In this episode, we talk about deglobalization and Wall Street, the threats AI and tech pose to investment banking, risk management in private credit, and rich people's attitudes towards taxes. Plus, Lloyd shares some of what he left out of the book and he explains why he doesn't tweet more. (Source: Bloomberg)

The illiquidity premium Money Stuff this week has mostly been about capturing the illiquidity premium. On Tuesday, I argued<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/khFVe-q5IL6ke8t4KM6BprtWjiV7q6ufGJrCfYTJAURJjlhQz5EbbL06HdUM41YfexhqTt7cjIimTtdYBgWif4xLiNcIG2AE0JB9AM2pE_L-KLKzY85zQts6vpIwQ9UELVETuYegbT-HceWTD4mjcHBmmpgM94FFofIGrtm5jdwhYX4I7OrUaUicNL42km358nbfQTHW_rcpv7lirME3BmIf8-xu5w18V0cIizan5i1G4WOs8AtiiN-0fJ9VAZdkd6EfULsV6a0RUelxoP0PIvyWp1dujjX3tp1CUQqo7myaFH2T7TEgLQFJQ4aL17v_uS__zSFpu9FS4oCnuAcgZT7qs203ZMRoLfSwXH3s3D_UN-LmUl1qLU9BsQ/hKvAKC4-siGbkMpwLoZBIazaDpqiCX6l/18> that pooled retirement savings vehicles like pension funds and annuity companies have predictable cash needs and can lock up a lot of their money for the long term to earn high returns, while individual retirement savers can never be sure they wont need their money back tomorrow and so demand more liquid investments. On Wednesday, we discussed<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/KdnNOwxBGeBNVbcQUWPwie5Gh_un59ETTQpiKkGbAdP-ZVL-dLfLPOdyuOTvDiB30BY1mvodhWc-4CSfsK4uQx__Ed9En7JDj3fQ6vAmMQN6w3M1dT-dLzi3d-OYi3V9IYrVdDPSFHcGn3G2rMViaffj5RKg7zpn22np--baCiTPTahjPV0X-5Fgc8KcSWK30ufjRYoWKSIfXeGJZP3mIpYW4aSfMBnPPoVBksT1Sv9MByY5-ngEhhSTi2C8opysxGXUYt6iyNtUqRbLmTLXLTDzxn2rK-siqXtKHvPSp4Aual9caFWNlJz6jis7UAR2HkQZ6rQlTjJwTgoP9giWyDbqALHV0Vf8tkhUY8z--MwZJlg_bcnORwKrQQ/9aa3dMrrGlZ4uwVwqVZLx4XEcwrwkdYq/18> how those individual savers withdrew a lot of money from a Blackstone Group Inc. private credit business development company called BCRED, in part because of credit worries (loans might default, etc.) but also in part because of liquidity worries (people are suddenly paying attention to the fact that it is sometimes hard for individual investors to get their money out of private BDCs). I argued that, if you are a professional investor who thinks the credit worries arent too serious, this could be a good buying opportunity. It is conventional to assume that there is such a thing as an illiquidity premium: Investors who lock their money up for a long time sacrifice some flexibility, and thus should demand a higher return than investors who can get their money back whenever. We have occasionally discussed<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/vxV8dcmgAaOa_kzMrFCdeQZim13bECGtGyPKYDqs0BhcolNykLmj5kVehuPCC0LVZzw2L2DDO79r0v597_jmI4v5gMLZGLu1Ioy6L0n82U90076oXkpe4QZTn31XOLeQTL8WHMTkqWDZrRKmh6YE4sW0vZ2nCDEoFI7KW-Wb5hAjS0G3IAkw8Hp0glR8Moe8SM6z1fg8_5QldAwAckRL7whiHS_YpOXtJ-u8lVmsKI_8pYQmY5i_vTbVt_5oPSaIs3Zm27I8iArjDQxYH0F8bPUIQgPNS8Fl8VPYeDhxDpBQXU2ytzPzMYYYxCsgvfxbiw5vJcUO2NEo1ziOZIy7D2X7uK63SwdkDgadq-jJWmdczzCl9xa9OHa22w/7wjxH6vhyJpPthi8IxXrShzkYJIt-qrZ/18> Cliff Asnesss clever argument<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/Jd_65Jko3Hnja7XHnX8UoxsoJ9j3Qs88JnKk1ABqlFnX8q0uvw9LoBFNkL9kBFZZvEhLxFme0i6dfbZ7bsbDzwsAPZQwSuY3ASw1MYpifbt5fRiy_2xdIJNl-0K5LdySmkFsHcnuR_VzQNQ-tFkqhNhBuKBbDTZ4MktLZsAQGpyt6oQDgp7LsnjkfX813VdsMInUyE1l0FdVYgleFMdUOCklCHET2TmmYIv_6goxHoQUDYz7jst0onIIw2pfoCJ75WBf9gGN5OGSGoNLI-Bd3uzN-gqA6cxFVTGq4rvHb1An1puAmsHxV-DTB2nLlOvLADZRpVJm-BFc5Uh8ijI5Sd-H9iJWsuCseIKP99OffdIMuGBGu05aMZfwtQ/nw7vhUBiveX4q5o71bV2WgeiIi6lOd9H/18> that actually its the reverse  that investors love to own assets that dont trade, because then they dont have to stress out all the time about the assets prices, so they should accept a lower return for illiquid assets  but surely this week there is an illiquidity premium. Right now, individual investors in private BDCs seem to be reacting to headlines about how BDCs might be limiting redemptions; they think hmm I dont want my redemptions to be limited so they try to take out their money. [1] They are demonstrating a demand for liquidity, and if you are willing to provide that liquidity  to give them their money back and lock up your own money for a while  then you should be able to get paid. For legal and marketing reasons, a lot of the big private credit firms cant do exactly that  they cant just go out to their own BDC customers and say hey I see you want out, thats fine, Ill cash you out at 80 cents on the dollar  but other people could. Specifically, last month Saba Capital Management and Cox Capital Partners announced an opportunistic tender offer<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/sqFKRxclLolQG9lvreDmVfIWrzhrDJvBss-8F7r0BVHuKcgXJ6rXgZhjkv1nsJfBhoBFqEo0L0oxqy2wuSbyZRQPjDAA3qjT9fA3UK-QeScruLuNwzZSWM_JhHE0JsvcC_jfKAw1PvC25s9JMS7ODMyOJoY5j44wTn_lnM6r92ZTu70cUAdJRE8S9SQM9VZNgam2Cx-3-3tL8LD1OoL7B7ZeMTvzQ0le0ZdCj-4H65gQ1fdaZMhvkXu0CoX9r9mAWqeTzFAgtXpBPqbzW_HSnnH9zRipvFAsNc2tnnQKphyR_8A64kJvuRfvLUML6MhakkOem1pWDMA2s__SZsTuSo_cfxpczrkfRam4DUhRv0CJrNcvAYp1o_s4PjY/bClnF7tmBJ5HaTFWNzYhjDRVsIOIoO8u/18> for a Blue Owl Capital Inc. BDC called OBDC II, as well as a few other Blue Owl BDCs, with an offer price thats expected to be at a 20% to 35% discount to net asset values. This strikes me as a smart trade: You cant measure it exactly, but intuitively it sure seems like the illiquidity premium in private BDCs blew out over the last few weeks, and Saba and Cox might reasonably think well, well sell liquidity high, and the premium will come down and well make a big profit. (The risk here is not so much the liquidity premium will keep going up as it is actually the credit is worse than we think. It is hard to isolate the illiquidity premium, though I guess you could hedge out the credit.) It is also a good bit of trolling; the implicit message is something like Blue Owl wont give you your money back but we will, for a price. I dont know if theyll actually get any shares in their tender offer. Blue Owl is giving OBDC II investors their money back<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/8Xs9aCgGQlSskt9LYqmQFV5nMrzh-0FQlaRMdeQ3776c6shwfAkRlFuB0o5eypWnII_eIHEIQlQwBGYS3HqKXtnXhBWZ8hl_tBMk0jzbKkgPXE1xIMgTggDdt8I4oxY-3Q5NU31zNs7AwF3-nuJeogoanxSBHOUra4wKY6FY_mckp_IOvx5B0U0Ji8qg9ccrykR76aYK1T48Q0V4Oj1l6oEBHbuAN-G-5OHTgENQcO0mZO2daulDqrJsNVUIZO9zPXD5zOXSMU5DAQvB4cxl9EFefPpu-toeylB8nmxIguRqVMpy5duuuwUkGof4apLuYuJqC7O-k84ya_WbUkcItxhCsAm1wIHN8awsTKByd3qTf-oiEYlCN0w4G78/on6c5CE4zRKBGKt9tyjfr_e2rQy11OJL/18> over time, and it previously offered them the chance to get all their money back at a 20% discount<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/IdsQJE2k7id5kVv7YPJdboQpPS2xnHODRmeswqG5HPbi2gRFFcE2OSefhSncezO1NySPgEtN4e-QSKt6QJ0UdMS53L1bPdvo-w8Qjyo45qq_3P3fO7QWZCxfeD0XhRED2TjNTMWEjEydq5kXcFK2HIxI7xOvkR0DzGNWE8dSdGdwLXDvW2JIkkoqN1VFaPpGmZg___5XOsGwjQsSI7b1i0kC44tVUfaQXbSvI78VOn0BJEpaBsAMWBett-SCQEhSurpY8_7L3fnNWXTjTsf-fusFXovQoPwJZLZwynK9P3EjdPEUfhYPz2jyJPPl8mFXhxNBHfApgNsQcesHUJqSfKVgyMwVJlmpOB99nzyEgatc4yOcpQMJ94NTCZY/HB4f1KzRocUJ9zQUN7wuPNSi2Y04x-da/18>, but they said no to that; why would they say yes to Saba and Cox? Anyway this is partly a story about Blue Owl and Blackstone and private credit and the structure of non-traded BDCs, but more broadly it is a story about the illiquidity premium as a market-wide factor, about individual investors general demand for liquidity. The Saba and Cox trade is not just about trolling Blue Owl; it is structurally a bet on the illiquidity premium. You could scale that trade up and buy retail illiquidity wherever you can get it. Bloombergs Loukia Gyftopoulou and Patrick Clark report today<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/akhmw0UmFr8mDivgIQbWxb77rOxDbb7tWNGeCp1Lx3eN1HOh4ecjWG7sX_tgFmd1TV0l56GK59Bv1R-SsH5T1nlswHhgBTavO9HqROvg8A_8eCg6AdrPe1r__368-s9Hds9i4g1Hd0DkqTXVBQq3rrzybFjEmRYk67WUSPGfw6mj1zJ1GkufvlMxDZoXZAkRAbQwFeSRxqv6H82iw_-WBA45jSgpnZvZtzmCxZcBeGW6KQDe45eJgl5p1qQO3911-Y0vOWaEw20JUrvBPd9K0Ap0znuOW_HJzxddMTcWOojrLfgNDP2212-ngd7Ir-EnlsYJ0SJlo3HF5yPBDVtEa1jmNuPigcSI33oQNZ0xfhFveAMTeTH2JkOLcUE/L33Nfpg7q552oiyNXOaGfllYOXbD0nIn/18>: Boaz Weinsteins Saba Capital Management and Cox Capital Partners have started a tender offer for Starwood Capital Groups real estate investment trust, less than two weeks after the firms proposed buying shares of some Blue Owl Capital Inc. funds. Saba and Cox are offering to buy about 5.4% of the outstanding Class S and Class I shares of Starwood Real Estate Income Trust, at discounts of 28.6% and 24.4%, respectively, from their Feb. 12 price, according to a statement Thursday. SREIT, as its known, tightened limits on investors ability to pull money from the fund in May 2024, at a time when higher-for-longer interest rates had ground real estate markets to a halt. It lifted the restrictions slightly in June. Does the constant retail buy-the-dip bid insulate the market against volatility? Dispersion Two weeks ago, I would have said that there are two main theses about the US stock market: 1. Artificial intelligence will eat everything. Every company in every industry will be replaced by AI<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/wGWaqC_SqY4OOZXwXa3zh23zRkiyR14Mf2b3E3Wx3o_lCSS1pjOz7w7d4LneVM-F2fIiQnhII0H4DWCDAynrTwYijtTYFTIYDT6guU1-YvJ7-BaVi0a3muQIB_Qz-Ctz96rxBfoH4pIey4eOw1953-xjRTuCZXSVrO1nTQoLoJ_C7Ewrgr1IU-YXDY43ATZElD6YgK5PVMWC3djOMhAa8z89QeHW4VrUWzZ_FpJT0hjbFgECQoWakhKgzp72uh0GI65WrGDKIRVjzddalePh0OUJeA-ZXiCo-srdnMkn18luhSTQM58uBjePN547mdbxjG-lgflWY9g6r4kU1a--TwASAjnm0agB8Y93B-s4M4ZejP_mgB-mvexmRhg/IgiWvus8fzfVl6TA5hmRAJVs50MpNzk0/18>, and trillions of dollars of revenue that previously went to software companies or financial services companies or whatever will be redirected to a handful of companies  AI labs, electric utilities, Nvidia  in the AI supply chain. 2. Artificial intelligence is a bubble. The companies in the AI supply chain are raising umpteen gazillion dollars of debt to build data centers and power plants with no clear business model and with lots of circular deals, it is all overhyped, and eventually it will collapse. These theses are basically opposites, so it is tempting to assume that they cover 100% of the possible outcomes. Also, AI companies in some loose sense represent a huge chunk of US equity market capitalization, so you might casually make some assumption like either half of the market will go up a lot and the other half will go down a lot, or else the first half will go down a lot and the second half will go up a lot. Either way, the overall market might not change too much, but there will be a lot of dispersion: These are not generally theses about the overall level of stock prices, but rather about which particular stocks will have high prices and which will have low prices. The nice thing about this schematic description is that you can bet on dispersion directly. You dont have to choose a thesis, AI will be big or no it wont. You can bet on either AI will be big or it wont. That is, you can make a bet of the form some stocks will go up a lot, and other stocks will go down a lot, and they will offset each other so that the overall stock market doesnt go up or down all that much. This is called a dispersion trade. The normal way to do it is to sell a lot of index stock options (which become more valuable when the stock index moves up or down a lot) and buy a lot of options on all of the individual stocks in the index (which become more valuable when those individual stocks move up or down a lot). You can do this in a hedged way so that you are not betting on the overall price level of the stock market, or on the overall volatility of the stock market. Instead, it is a bet on correlation: If the individual stocks are all very volatile but in different directions, then the single-stock options will be worth a lot (high volatility) but the index will not be volatile (the moves will cancel out), the index options will not be worth much and youll make money. If the individual stocks all move together, though, then the index will be just as volatile as the individual stocks (all of the moves will reinforce each other), the index options will be very valuable, and you will lose money. We have talked about the dispersion trade<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/No-xKZyIXsprEiV-ZyfBdn54h64c_E-rvGBmiiHfPk7_N6iQpOSPZUpts971W_J8VygccID4oAr8zQfo5ffuubg1LvhHP8Erre2A0Y2URULXm4rpAKqkqN8EShcofm5hSd9wR5hWRgEHI7HIdT0iiPM6zuq4GqQnIq8W7yqML86otIq8tMO_OrhdztqRLeClk5Ba01vi0rOVc-7847bn9umkPWYqVqQAiS0o2pPJpvn4oqTvnTg17PrC6EBE6Mq1lXtTdGnzOnvg-ESltdfDK6MHE374VTU5jNhjjRbioybStgp7Ug9NlpIXTD3lRApo8jH0OdDo9vD9MMtieQgzmixFJQgoeHajDuzffXTYswyxOs7IeWBe0YokAD8/eQ5crt3ZQ_oEcEUzXtX1LAKbWcLqy-HV/18> generally as a sort of structural feature of the stock market: Some real-money end-user investors like to sell single-stock options (buy-write strategies, etc.), others like to buy index options (crash insurance), so hedge funds step in to take the other sides of those trades, effectively betting against correlation. With Bitcoin and with cash, you cannot expect everyone to discriminate perfectly between good and bad money: It is so culturally and practically important that money be fungible that most people are not going to check their Bitcoins provenance, or their bills serial numbers, against the Index of Forbidden Money. Generally speaking you shouldnt have an Index of Forbidden Money. If you do, that is going to make commerce slower and less certain. Fungibility really is the point of money, and if you make your money nonfungible then it becomes less useful. While thousands swarmed the site to pick up the banknotes in one of Latin Americas poorest nations, authorities have tried to burn and destroy the new cash, arresting dozens and raiding homes in a rushed hunt for the missing bills. That has sent Bolivians into a frenzy. No longer able to quickly tell if a banknote is valid or voided and fearing the crackdown, businesses dont know what bills to accept anymore, leaving customers frustrated and panicked that their real money is now worthless. ... The bank has said that all the bills being carried by the plane  which were denominated in 10, 20 and 50 bolivianos  belonged to a Series B that include 9-digit serial numbers. Initially, the central bank suspended the use of any Series B bill for 48 hours. Now, its released a mobile app for vendors to manually input the serial numbers to verify if a bill is legitimate or voided. It doesnt matter if the serial number is valid, they wont take it, said Sonia Queveriano, 50, who sells fresh juices in La Paz but has not been able to buy fruit for her business using Series B bills. Its unfortunate that we have to pay for this, as if we had gone to steal that money. Vendors acknowledge theyre being extra cautious and would rather avoid Series B bills altogether. The risk of a voided bill is one thing, but theres also a chance that other sellers wont take any Series B bills themselves. Yes if you have to type the 9-digit serial number into an app to decide if the money is good or not, it becomes less useful as money. title: Oil Tops $81, Trump Replaces Noem at DHS | Bloomberg Businessweek Daily 3/5/2026
content: On today's episode of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily, Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec discuss today's market action with stocks moving lower, bonds sliding, and oil topping $80 a barrel for the first time since January 2025. Bloomberg Economics Chief Geoeconomics Analyst Jennifer Welch joins to discuss inflationary risks stemming from Iran, and Aaron Kennon of Clear Harbor Asset Management weighs in on investor strategy. Then, Bloomberg News White House Correspondent Jeff Mason discusses President Trump removing Kristi Noem at DHS. Plus, Bloomberg News Chief Correspondent for Private Capital Davide Scigliuzzo as private credit concerns continue. Finally, Dr. Lauren Osborne, Vice Chair of Clinical Research, Department of OBGYN at Weill Cornell Medicine, joins to discuss women's postpartum health and treatments. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Private Credit Concerns Grow as Execs See Tough Times Ahead
content: Concerns have been bubbling up over the $1.8 trillion private credit market in recent weeks, with investors spooked in part by the risk of artificial intelligence on some borrowers and worries about valuations. Last month, a Blue Owl Capital Inc. fund opted to halt quarterly redemptions and started selling assets to return money to investors. This week, Blackstone Inc.’s flagship private credit fund allowed investors to redeem a record 7.9% of shares. JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon has spoken of failed corporate borrowers as “cockroaches,” suggesting there could be more. Bloomberg News Chief Correspondent for Private Capital Davide Scigliuzzo joins Bloomberg Businessweek Daily to discuss. He speaks with Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec. (Source: Bloomberg)

Europe’s neobanks have had a mixed history when it comes to expanding to the US. Monzo, for instance, retreated from the market in 2021 after it became clear US regulators weren’t going to approve a local licence. And despite operating in the US since 2020, the country is yet to form a meaningful part of Revolut’s revenue. But after the re-election of US president Donald Trump brought in a wider deregulatory push, things are changing. UK neobank Starling is exploring expanding to the US by obtaining a local banking licence, according to Sifted reporting in June. And in October, the FT reported Monzo is weighing up a fresh US banking licence application. The one on the right tends to indicate a broader mean-reversion trade, such as the S&P 500<https://substack.com/redirect/14f13931-3018-4752-ae62-4860b01b370d?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Between these extremes ought to be a diversity of pricing trends honed from rigorous analysis of all possible futures, each weighted by probability through dynamic price discovery. At least that’s the theory. It’s not been working that way for a while. Take, for example, Korean equities<https://substack.com/redirect/b09222e0-0232-4a7f-8638-6b13b96b76c2?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. The Kospi 200 index hit a record high on Tuesday, entered a technical bear market halfway through Wednesday, and set the floor for a new bull market early on Thursday. Even for a notoriously choppy index, that’s a lot: [https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!M2xd!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcfd278c6-c657-46b4-b87a-a6617aa60870_1020x691.png]<https://substack.com/redirect/2efea6b4-1e1e-40a1-97f4-accb1d532514?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> As tends to be the way, explanations abound. Korean stocks went up on AI-related chip shortages<https://substack.com/redirect/31563d79-54c5-4165-944d-5093e5794878?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, fresh interest in heavy industry<https://substack.com/redirect/fa955270-661d-4f51-9a1d-1cb58cd3993c?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, a possible narrowing of conglomerate discounts<https://substack.com/redirect/25f6cad4-b01a-4c10-90db-368f5d2c88bb?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, and K-Pop Demon Hunters<https://substack.com/redirect/81026da7-6dc9-40be-a4d2-670026809978?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Korean company earnings will more than double in 2026<https://substack.com/redirect/ef62294d-420f-4a37-ba0d-c015ce93d707?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, consensus expectations having shot higher in recent months. Jitters only surfaced when bombs started dropping 4,000 miles away<https://substack.com/redirect/18747675-7396-4bd7-8991-02d6b9eaa5f9?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. And with any rapid repricing comes volatility. Current uncertainty levels for Korean equities are rivalling the Great Financial Crisis, which is an odd thing to say about some memory chip supply bottlenecks and corporate stewardship code revisions, but there we are: [https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Xb3u!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F11f4b131-d1ed-4ec7-92c1-1621b4385e5c_1224x755.png]<https://substack.com/redirect/f83742ff-eace-4375-a1c6-dbb8b371fa40?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> It’s mixed news for Korea’s punter army, who in recent years have been weaned off property investments and into stocks. President Lee Jae Myung this week activated a $68bn plunge protection fund<https://substack.com/redirect/118d2208-563c-419a-a3cc-aaeb09907bc6?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> to quell panic selling, having last week led by example and sold a rental apartment to buy ETFs<https://substack.com/redirect/808125ba-3e7a-4205-8ced-7fb2e67d3956?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. “At the small downtown office of Mirae Asset Securities, scores of clients hurriedly lined up to get their money out,” reports Bloomberg<https://substack.com/redirect/b945b92a-f4e8-4f68-8c95-06f86a4c719f?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>: What the episode shows is just how fast a market dominated by leveraged, margin-fuelled bets and amped up by frenzied day traders can sour, exposing the risks of an investment culture that had come to treat borrowing as a sure thing to bigger gains. True, though it also shows the rapid flip-flop between greed and fear. A mania among Korea’s retail investors only really caught hold in February<https://substack.com/redirect/71630afb-e8c0-447d-b2c0-d619e0dda4c5?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, and while their leverage levels are high in absolute terms, they’re unremarkable relative to market value<https://substack.com/redirect/8bae963f-8552-41a2-82e6-44a187d6b57a?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Some tourist capital will have been caught up into Korea’s recent rally, though risks can be overstated when retail and institutions are taking opposite sides of the bet: [https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!s3H-!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fef737ee3-edcf-4e96-bced-7ee57455589d_1307x684.png]<https://substack.com/redirect/477e7c47-5c87-4f38-9749-99b4b6466ffe?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> All of which brings us back to the diagram at the top of the page. Powering the hand-crafted spike and sawtooth charts are two factors: momentum and mean reversion. In both cases, they’re amplified by retail and professionals taking opposite sides. Last month’s AI disruption scare<https://substack.com/redirect/d2632d71-5ea9-4ad1-acfd-524e838b8c48?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> is a prime example. “Retail’s appetite to buy the dip has remained a dominant force in early-2026 flows,” says Citadel Securities<https://substack.com/redirect/86727ec1-f746-40de-8c81-d17501a8291b?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, which reports net buying of US equities by individuals at nearly a five-year high. As Matt Levine writes<https://substack.com/redirect/717a75d1-fd9b-497e-aa91-999a29b25b2b?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>: This is an interesting stock market story: Are retail investors the ultimate value investors in the stock market? Does the constant retail buy-the-dip bid insulate the market against volatility? Maybe it does until it doesn’t. There’s a dampening effect to having lots of retail money sloshing around<https://substack.com/redirect/1276a1bb-1a29-436b-bc84-9f115b4bc320?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, but add a product shortage or an inflation scare, and it remains a volatile accelerant. Volatility is suppressed until it’s not. You can’t choose which chart you’ll get. There’s no BTFD without YOLO and FUD. title: BlackRock $26 Billion Private Credit Fund Limits Withdrawals
content: BlackRock curbed withdrawals from one of its biggest private credit funds after client requests for redemptions spiked, the latest sign of investor anxiety about the $1.8 trillion private credit industry. The firm’s $26 billion HPS Corporate Lending Fund, one of the largest non-traded business development companies, said in a statement Friday that shareholders requested 9.3% of their shares, but management decided to cap the repurchases at 5%. place in the world to be a female entrepreneur, its flagship fund of funds is yet to deploy any capital. The ‘Women Backing Women’ fund is raising £250m to invest in female fund managers in the UK to in turn back female-led startups - but hasn’t made any investments to date. title: FW: 09/03/26: Auxmoney gründet Rückversicherer - so funktioniert der Restschuld-Case
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Monday, 9 March 2026 06:34:58 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 09/03/26: Auxmoney gründet Rückversicherer  so funktioniert der Restschuld-Case Außerdem: Fintech-Personalien, Matthiesens Abgang, Die LLB in Deutschland [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/57197114-2df1-d3d8-6586-607a05ca5755.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=b9a73a5a7f&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Auch Auxmoney gründet Rückversicherer  so funktioniert jetzt der Restschuld-Case Die Deutsche Bank ist nicht der typische Konsumfinanzierer da draußen. Als wir neulich allerdings über die Pläne der Commerzbank berichteten<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=2e6aaf754c&e=8f69674dd2>, einen eigenen Rückversicherer zu gründen, und im Zuge der Recherche lernten, dass die Deutsche Bank schon seit Jahrzehnten einen solchen Rückversicherer unterhält  da staunten wir nicht schlecht. Denn: Die DB Re SA (so heißt die entsprechende Deutsche-Bank-Tochter) generierte zuletzt fast die Hälfte ihrer Bruttobeiträge aus einer einzigen Policen-Kategorie, und zwar aus "Zahlungsschutz-Versicherungen". Sprich: Es geht ganz offenbar um Restschuld-Versicherungen. Also um Policen, die den Kreditnehmer gegen Tod, Arbeitslosigkeit oder Krankheit absichern sollen. Und die gerade bei Ratenkrediten umstritten sind, da sie als überteuert und intransparent gelten. Was uns nun allerdings noch mehr erstaunte als die Erkenntnis, dass die Restschuld-Versicherung im Geschäftsjahr 2024 satte 48% des Beitragsvolumens des Deutsche-Bank-Rückversicherers ausmachten  das war die Tatsache, dass die DB Re SA das entsprechende Geschäft erst 2023 aufgenommen hatte (und damit rund ein Jahr, nachdem die Bundesregierung beschlossen hatte, die Vermittlungsprovision bei Restschuld-Versicherungen auf 2,5% des abgesicherten Darlehensvertrags zu deckeln). Das bedeutet: 1.) Angesichts des zeitlichen Zusammenhangs drängt sich der Verdacht auf, dass das eine eine Reaktion auf das andere war; und 2.) In dem Geschäft steckt offenbar so viel Wumms, dass es in weniger als 24 Monaten zum weitaus größten Geschäftsfeld aufstieg. Jedenfalls, damit nun zu Auxmoney. Denn: Anders als die Deutsche Bank ist das Düsseldorfer Fintech ein gerade reinrassiger (und brutal wachsender) Konsumfinanzierer. Und wie neue Recherchen von Finanz-Szene zeigen, hat auch Auxmoney still und leise einen eigenen Rückversicherer gegründet. Und zwar 2023, also in jenem Jahr, in dem auch die DB Re SA ganz offenbar begann, Ratenkredite rückzuversichern. Erfahren Sie hier, was Auxmoney konkret macht. Wie das Geschäft binnen kürzester Zeit zum Ergebnistreiber aufstieg. Wie das Zusammenspiel mit dem Erstversicherer funktioniert. Und welch überragende Rolle (auch für andere Banken) ein fast unbekanntes Unternehmen aus dem niederrheinischen Hilden bei alldem spielt. Der digitale Euro wird alles dominieren? Die Debatte ist laut, meinungsstark - und wird in Teilen zu isoliert geführt. Doch wer sieht den Wald vor lauter Bäumen? Warum es nicht um Sieger, sondern um Rollen, Übergänge und Systemlogik geht, analysiert OSTHAVEN hier.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=964eb21af4&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Der durch und durch überraschende Abgang des Deutschbankers Matthiesen. Wenn Ole Matthiesen die Deutsche Bank unbedingt verlassen wollte, dann hätte er eigentlich genügend Zeit dafür gehabt. Schließlich hat der 41-Jährige fast sein gesamtes Berufsleben bei den Frankfurtern zugebracht und dabei einen bemerkenswerten Aufstieg hingelegt: vom jugendlichen Einsteiger (2008) zum Global Head of Cash Management (2019) zum Asien-Chef der Unternehmensbank (seit 2022) zum Co-Chef der gesamten Unternehmensbank (seit Anfang Januar)  auf Augenhöhe mit Ex-HVB-CEO Michael Diederich (er ist der andere Co-Chef) und nur noch eine Ebene unterm Vorstand, zudem Mitglied des einflussreichen Group Management Committee ... ... Doch ausgerechnet jetzt, nur wenige Wochen nach der vermeintlichen Krönung seiner Blitzkarriere  zieht's Matthiesen unvermittelt weg ("um sich neuen Aufgaben zu widmen"), wie die Deutsche Bank am Freitag überraschend mitteilte. Immerhin, einen adäquaten Nachfolger gibt es, nämlich Gerald Podobnik, bislang Finanzchef der Sparte, auch er ein Eigengewächs (Podobnik kam 2003 zur Deutschen Bank), auch er deutschsprachig, was bei der Besetzung offenkundig ein wichtiges Kriterium war. Das andere Kriterium (nachdem Vorvorgänger David Lynne die Sparte bis Ende 2025 von Singapur aus geführt hatte) lautete freilich, dass der Chef bzw. die Chefs der prestigeträchtigen Firmenkundensparte wieder von Frankfurt aus arbeiten sollen ... ... Das sollte auch für Matthiesen gelten, bei dessen Bestellung vor wenigen Wochen es explizit geheißen hatte, er werde von Singapur (wo er seit 2022 seinen Sitz hatte) "nach Frankfurt zurückkehren". Umso bemerkenswerter, dass im Umfeld der Deutschen Bank nun spekuliert wird, "private Gründe" könnten beim Weggang eine Rolle gespielt haben  sprich, dass Matthiesen nun doch lieber in Singapur bleiben wolle. Man darf jedenfalls gespannt sein, wo der bisherige Deutschbanker dann demnächst aufschlagen wird. Everything about private credit  its systemic safety, its light regulation, its go-anywhere investing approach, its high returns  flows from the fact that the investors cant get their money back whenever they want. Traditionally, the long-term locked-up investors were institutional investors who could easily bear the risk of not getting their money back for years: pensions, endowments, sovereigns, and especially life insurance and annuity companies, which have predictable long-term liabilities and which frequently are owned by the same asset managers that run the private credit funds. And there private credit was, in a paradise of low risk and high returns, when it made, collectively, a fateful decision. The decision was these long-term locked-up institutional investors are great, but really we should sell this stuff to retail. Why did the private credit industry decide to sell its stuff to individual retail investors? Here are four possible reasons: 1. Altruism: These institutional investors are getting such great returns from private credit; it is not fair for retail investors to miss out; we should let them in. 2. Growth: We have tapped out every last dollar of institutional capital, but individuals have trillions of dollars of retirement savings and almost no private credit. If we want to sell more private credit, we need to sell to them. 3. Top-ticking: Man, private credit is in a bubble and weve made a lot of really aggressive loans; who is going to hold the bag if not unsophisticated retail investors? 4. The squeezing of public asset managers. This is a subtler one, but big mutual fund managers have had a rough few years: Individual investors want extremely low-cost index funds, so it is harder and harder to make money<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/SjCosR74oIvJZnIoBwDd4Dq-z4m-ZHGGFYlec5YEgw3YnoLIY6F2srpdkqm3RGFVRtQjEs1cAvBosXNcg68lSfYCpo-a6ptkv2RtjMjQCMYYbR_cPA5--wj9408BVa0XqvMJ1iPb8xoeZNgqYDWl5lORV7FY9DBQwwe4iQyurZEl1aNW_zd781MXdsmReiSO5BJBMe13Tt3Nixr-gfilR5M0feKMmjBfcmtn40zrB-R-M2JCJRNxaqZS-JADHRjp7CcnbAvbrXLPoi-dZoOadogaxqSur__zE1U4mMhuqFI0J4Y_WD9kMCJlZx03Qv73NGKL7J2TA_sCBxNZVNi2nyywiUg7dai6T64l8vaHEZWOHZpTEgWR1a6WHGM/QiQo1BBTuAWRaiCzDvL228P4y8Nup-1y/18> by selling them mutual funds containing public stocks and bonds. Collectively, I think, that list of reasons should make you nervous. None of those reasons sounds great for credit discipline or returns. When private credit managers invest relatively small amounts of money for sophisticated institutional investors  in many cases, for their own balance sheets, in the form of their affiliated insurers  they can try to make only good loans and seek high rates of return. When they are looking to put trillions of dollars of retail money to work rapidly, you know, less so. But there was, it turns out, another reason to be nervous, one that I did not fully appreciate a year ago, which is that retail investors really do not like to lock up their money for the long term. If you raise money from a pension or an endowment or an annuity company, you say thanks, gonna make some seven-year loans, so Ill give you this money back in seven years, bye, and they leave you alone for seven years. Those investors should be willing to lock up their money for the long term, but they apparently arent, in part because of genuine risks to their cash needs (they might get sick and need cash, etc.) and in part for reasons of stereotypical retail-investor psychology (they might get nervous and pull their money when headlines are bad). And so when private credit funds raise money from individuals, it is generally in one of two ways: 1. Publicly-traded business development companies. (For boring legal and historical reasons, a retail-oriented private credit fund is called a business development company, or BDC.) These are closed-end funds with permanent capital that trade on the stock exchange. The private credit firm gets long-term locked-up capital (the investors cant withdraw their money), while the retail investors in the fund get instant total liquidity (they can sell their shares, on the stock exchange, whenever they want). For an industry that has ballooned to $1.8 trillion  and is on the cusp of prying open Americas 401(k)s and other retirement accounts  it was an uncomfortable step. It risks generating a backlash from retail investors who are growing increasingly anxious to access their money and, in so doing, reinforces the dangers long expressed by industry skeptics of selling illiquid assets to a twitchy customer base. But the move was also one that a number of executives, in private conversations, have said they were hoping an industry heavyweight like BlackRock would make, giving others cover to do the same.
