Among other things, fiduciaries must establish and follow processes to ensure that plan participants savings are not exposed to excessive levels of risk, and must monitor investment options to ensure that their fees, performance, and risk levels are appropriate for retirement savings. ERISA was designed to protect retirement security and requires fiduciaries to protect workers from risks that would undermine that goal . Climate change-related risk presents precisely that kind of threat: it is financially substantial, it is escalating, and it imperils the value and stability of investments across asset classes  causing both sudden and long-term harms. Defendants exposed employee retirement savings to significant, unreasonable climate-related financial riskapparently failing to employ any climate risk management strategy at all. A prime example of this failure is the inclusion of the Westwood Quality SmallCap Fund (the Westwood Fund or the Fund) as a fund option on the Companys 401(k) menu. The Westwood Fund is openly indifferent to climate risk: its managers declare that they neither model nor manage climate risk in the Funds portfolio. Unsurprisingly, this climate risk blindness has led the Fund to aggregate inordinate levels of climate-related financial risk across its investment sectors. Compared to its benchmark index, the Westwood Fund is more than twice as exposed to sectors that are particularly vulnerable to climate-related financial risk. This overweighting in risky sectors is bad enough, but even in sectors that should provide a hedge against climate risk, the Fund invests disproportionately in companies with high climate risk exposure. This is exactly the American Airlines case, but in reverse. People sued American for hiring an asset manager that considers ESG; now people are suing Cushman & Wakefield for hiring an asset manager that doesnt. May I sell you stock? In 2024, Bill Ackman came to the stock market<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/_olxoj7qQA0_8BE3MoTV2mccCFSkMbci9j1reX3hGN9kiz5wyhBSz6p1xvF5KS9VX5_zZ2ZdekwCTg636OfM6Z4rkc-l0iy9fJTnhloJersYSC_tg-XPHUYNGIX6qxOCv8hRHEE1BOPQtNc3a4-7AmTNJEgYRYeTJ6lhJ9T4-Rnlam20TfhMKJ9ABJxdPB10smJOTtXTuLPYKPFyqwrAVkgHFTxQnUwtuh04XQjHrokj3bCw9L_ZbSWYjdokOQkaPq_dfpumdSR84smIWgk44d71ImelHUWeneR1IUrX3R_CMgNJPdIRzExLogdz1biux_PWpRw3T3vVJHyGl9fudyO6LlKm8-YGcL3IEUax_ZkjLtB4ZpHmqKcovw/Lh1hue4Pv_V5VIfiAZp5G2UlJWp9iVVr/18> with a proposition: You could give him $50, and he would invest about $49 of it in some stocks for you. (The other $1 would go to underwriting fees. [1] ) This is called a closed-end fund, and Ackmans is called Pershing Square USA Ltd., or PSUS. How much is that proposition worth? How much should you pay for $49 worth of stocks selected for you by Bill Ackman? Some possible answers include: * $49, because $49 worth of stocks is worth $49; * less than $49, because Ackman will charge you fees for picking the stocks, which will reduce the value of your stake over time [2] ; or * more than $49, because Bill Ackman is good at picking stocks and will pick ones that go up more than the average stock. [3] Ackman obviously argued for more than $49, because he is quite confident in his ability to pick the stocks that go up. Others disagreed. Closed-end funds often trade at a discount to net asset value (i.e., less than $49), so it would not be unreasonable to worry that Ackmans would also trade at a discount. In fact Ackman already has a closed-end fund in Europe, called Pershing Square Holdings Ltd.<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/cWCWHXFEWUXbEAaKi00_ISvleMEJ2zToO1zfWhaRhYLX8vuPkiBOpqoK87SBFnhvo3-HR1wdSkb7TpkhSGBBb_jdr9trsVrFicTKMNsBx2WgnQvvXXPzdHoaqkv0x9HlHHUtoqM5QajqhOqB3joSGbGfUW27FYeh9zRvbWqe9MJl9YPMsYHtrzn8-xEWrUbea12bv4JPv48G8aECYOuwjcQcy61Fabo_XSDExFQDdx5_j1HdxWWjJNop1ihhdmTBk_EhJiP-Oa7qub47jM5EMDdrBt5_cruOT4HUrWdvduHWuzuRROGqBrgU0MvoH8UZqxVWzXJzwlgUEDD7EOUYHwDKC4wGwslr0Z3LGnsa4NcRlw0OZe30mvb4Yg/ZRCULttzE0h7bUY-cTHPbPyhP7LrBcbQ/18>, and it trades at a discount, so. This is a big problem when it comes to raising money. If Bill Ackman comes to you and says give me $50 to buy $49 worth of stocks, and you think that proposition is worth $52, you give him the $50 and everything is great. But if you think that proposition is worth $47, theres a problem. You cant give him $47 to buy $49 worth of stocks: Where would he get the other $2? (He could just buy $46 of stocks for you, but thats not worth $47  thats worth like $43. Etc.) Ackman can only raise new money from people who think that his fund is worth more than net asset value; he can only get this started by selling shares at a premium. Anyway this didnt work. Which stocks? How did they decide which stocks to buy? How did they coordinate to all buy the same stocks at the same time? Well, there were some online discussion boards  Reddits WallStreetBets forum was the most famous  and they got together there and talked explicitly about what to buy. This was important because they were mostly small investors. A big asset manager can buy a lot of stock and move the price, but a small retail investor cant. Millions of small retail investors acting together apparently can, but historically they typically didnt, because they had no way to coordinate: If I spend $1,000 to buy one stock and you spend $1,000 to buy another stock and someone else decides to sell those stocks, nothing really happens, but if we all agree to spend our $1,000 to buy the same stock on the same day it will go up. Social media provided a surprising new way for small-time retail investors to coordinate and, thus, to move stock prices. This phenomenon got the name meme stocks, which emphasizes the fun and arbitrary nature of the picks, but its also worth emphasizing the coordination. The abstract: Analyzing trading behavior in the binary option market for retail investors, we find that market participants purchase binary options although strictly dominant bull spreads are available at lower prices: 15% of S&P index, 19% of gold, and 25% of silver trades violate no-dominance conditions consistently across three different asset classes. Buyers of dominated binaries lose on average 34% of the contract price by forgoing the dominating product. We show that our results are consistent with retail investors valuing simple, easy-to-understand binary bets. That is, you can buy a binary option that pays out $100 if some index is above 1,000, and $0 if its below 1,000. Or you can buy a call spread that pays out at least as much as the binary option in every state of the world, say $0 if the index is below 800, $120 if its above 900, and a linearly increasing amount in between. The paper has a schematic diagram: [https://assets.bwbx.io/images/users/iqjWHBFdfxIU/iPucQpmN6X7I/v0/-1x-1.png] The dotted line is always better than the binary payoff. And they find that people pay less for the dominating bull spread than they do for the binary, for the pretty obvious reason that the bull spread is complicated, has different (always better) payoffs in different situations, requires you to buy multiple options and do math, etc., while the binary option is just you make money if yes and you lose your bet if no. Thats easier, so people pay more for it. It simplifies it in a way that everybody can really understand, so it takes out the intimidation factor of the markets. Goodman and Puri are making an academic point  a theoretically-grounded empirical impetus for research in behavioral finance which goes beyond historically pervasive utility frameworks  but of course I am more interested in the commercial point. The commercial point is that you should sell people binary options because they will overpay for them. If the CEO lied to reporters with a plan like a big magazine will publish a glowing profile of me, and investors will read that profile, and they will want to invest, and then I will go out and raise money from them without lying directly but relying on the glowing profile, then (1) that kind of does sound like securities fraud and (2) its absolutely part of what got, for instance, Elizabeth Holmes. [10] But if you lie to reporters and then publicly post a formal retraction before raising any more money, is that okay? I mean. Dont ask me. Dont ask ChatGPT either. Anyway TechCrunch reports that in June, Cluely raised a $15 million Series A from Andreessen Horowitz, and the allegedly misleading article came out in July. Maybe its fine. content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Wednesday, 11 March 2026 06:15:42 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 11/03/26: Wo der Geno-Gewinn herkommt, Berliner Fintech landet Funding Außerdem: Bafin fährt beim IBB vor, Private Equity greift nach Prüfverband [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/57197114-2df1-d3d8-6586-607a05ca5755.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=672774538c&e=8f69674dd2> Wieso die Volksbanken den Gewinn nochmal ausbauen (anders als wohl die Sparkassen) Wer in den letzten Wochen unsere Berichterstattung zur Bilanzsaison in den beiden Verbünden verfolgt hat (siehe vor allem das Stück > Wie sich die Gewinne von Sparkassen und Volksbanken verselbstständige<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=fc79ed5fd4&e=8f69674dd2>n)  den dürfte kaum überrascht haben, dass die BVR-Oberen bei ihrer gestrigen Bilanz-PK exzellente Zahlen im Gepäck hatten. Überraschend kam allenfalls, wie exzellent die Zahlen letztlich ausgefallen sind. Denn während die regionalen Sparkassen-Verbände zuletzt überwiegend von einer Verteidigung der Zinsergebnisse und damit der Betriebsergebnisse berichteten, haben die Volks- und Raiffeisenbanken den Zinsüberschuss im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr sogar nochmal signifikant ausgebaut  nämlich um 5% auf noch nie dagewesene 21,5 Mrd. Euro. Mit der Folge, dass das Betriebsergebnis sogar um ein Zehntel auf 9,5 Mrd. Euro nach Bewertung anschwoll. Auf die Frage, wie dieses Kunststück gelang, gibt es nun drei Antworten, nämlich zwei naheliegende (die so ähnlich auch auf die Sparkassen zutreffen dürften) und eine für die Connaisseure. Lesen Sie hier unsere Analyse der 2025er-Zahlen der genossenschaftlichen Primärebene, einschließlich der sehr interessanten Fragen, warum sich eigentlich das Provisionsgeschäft seit Jahren so anämisch entwickelt und warum bei den Sparkassen die Sachkosten explodieren, bei den Genossen aber ganz und gar nicht: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=bc34c78df7&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/055d3feb-d58f-c3ea-7e48-6323dfd6b403.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=6bbf3696ca&e=8f69674dd2> Wero ersetzt die girocard? Der digitale Euro wird alles dominieren? Die Debatte ist laut, meinungsstark - und wird in Teilen zu isoliert geführt. Doch wer sieht den Wald vor lauter Bäumen? Warum es nicht um Sieger, sondern um Rollen, Übergänge und Systemlogik geht, analysiert OSTHAVEN hier.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c7a8f187af&e=8f69674dd2> Primärbanken-Monitor (#2) Die BBBank ist extrem offensiv unterwegs  aber was hat sie wirklich drauf? (frei zugänglich) Jahrelang war die BBBank der Inbegriff des stillen genossenschaftlichen Nischenplayers. Ein fraglos großes Institut (mit 22,5 Mrd. Euro Bilanzsumme die Nr. 2 im jüngsten BVR-Ranking)  aber auch eines, das sich als bundesweit tätige Direktbank mit solider Stammklientel (das zweite der drei "Bs" steht für "Beamte") geräuschlos durch Zeit, Luft und Branche bewegte. Vielleicht mal abgesehen von der Sache mit dem Hauskredit für den damaligen Finanzminister Christian Lindner. Und dem schmeichelnden Grußwort, das der FDP-Politiker für eine Jubiläumsfeier des Instituts gehalten hatte. Da geriet die BBBank dann doch mal ins Scheinwerferlicht. Naja, jedenfalls: Die "Causa Grußwort" ist längst vergessen. Die Scheinwerfer allerdings  die sind zurück. Zuerst schnappte sich das in Karlsruhe ansässige Institut (das erste "B" steht für "Badische") die PSD Berlin-Brandenburg. Und zum 1. Januar dieses Jahres verleibte sie sich auch noch die PSD Bank Hessen-Thüringen ein  ein Vorgang, der manchen Insider vermuten ließ, dass Vorstandschef Oliver Lüsch sogar schon den nächsten Streich vorbereiten könnte (siehe -> BBBank übernimmt zweite PSD Bank  folgt bald schon die dritte?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=daadf01a69&e=8f69674dd2>). Die BBBank ist, kurz gesagt, also gerade wahnsinnig offensiv unterwegs da draußen. Deshalb war es höchste Zeit, sich das Institut mal ein wenig genauer anzuschauen. Für den zweiten Teil unseres neuen "Primärbanken-Monitors" haben wir die "BBBB" (also die BBBank-Bilanzen) einmal in den Röntgenapparat geschoben. Unsere Analyse aus dem Dezember, jetzt für kurze Zeit vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (10 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=6f6244386e&e=8f69674dd2> Heute im Premium-Newsletter * Exklusiv: Private Equity greift nach genossenschaftlichem Prüfungsverband  der BVR gibt sich (noch) gelassen * Exklusiv: Parallel zum abrupten Vorstandswechsel  die Bafin fährt beim Internationalen Bankhaus Bodensee vor * Exklusiv: Wie Berenberg nach der Abgangswelle im Wealth Management die Reihen aufzufüllen versucht Jetzt Premium-Abonnent werden und unbegrenzt Finanz-Szene lesen  zu den Angeboten geht's hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=8c748e568f&e=8f69674dd2>. Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/ff23bf10-d905-d852-0d1a-7d6e08bdd499.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=d73f933339&e=8f69674dd2> Jetzt neu bei Finanz-Szene  unser Private-Banking-Letter: Was ist los bei Berenberg, Bethmann und Co.? Welche Pläne verfolgen Sparkassen und Volksbanken im Private Banking? Und was setzen Deutsche und Coba der Wealth-Management-Offensive der großen Auslandsbanken entgegen? Die Antworten gibt es künftig einmal monatlich in unserem Private-Banking-Letter. Hier kostenlos anmelden: Finanz-Szene<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0a617d9026&e=8f69674dd2> News * Während die Sparkassen in der Debatte um ein regulatorisches "Kleinbanken-Regime" einen Positionswechsel sondieren (siehe unseren Scoop von letzter Woche<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=73a6f43d56&e=8f69674dd2>), hält der BVR unbeirrt am leverage-ratio-basierten Ansatz fest. Diese Stoßrichtung gelte für die gesamte Deutsche Kreditwirtschaft (also auch für den DSGV ...), versicherte BVR-Präsidentin Marija Kolak gestern  dass "auf Arbeitsebene" auch andere Überlegungen angestellt würden, sei ein "normaler Prozess". Kurz Die Aktien von Deutsche Bank (+3,4% auf 27,46 Euro) und Commerzbank (+4,5% auf 31,72 Euro) haben sich am Dienstag deutlich erholt +++ Die Deutsche Bank will ihren Bonus-Pool fürs abgelaufene Geschäftsjahr um "mehr als 5%" (verglichen mit dem Vorjahr) anheben, berichtet "Bloomberg" Wussten Sie schon? ... dass "Barzahlen"-Gründer Achim Bönsch, Sebastian Seifert und Andreas Veller für ihr frisch gegründetes neues Fintech (siehe hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c1b933e9c3&e=8f69674dd2>) jetzt auch Funding bekommen? Wie die Kollegen von "Finance Forward"<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=77268c5155&e=8f69674dd2> berichten, haben die Berliner insgesamt 3,3 Mio. Euro Eigenkapital eingeworben, unter anderem vom New Yorker VC Motive Ventures (wo ja Finleap-Gründer Ramin Niroumand mittlerweile angedockt hat). Favoriten 1. Private credit marks Lets say I lend a software company $100 for five years at 8% interest. I give the company $100 in cash, and it gives me back a note promising to pay me back, which I enter into my accounting system as a $100 asset. The next day, Anthropic releases some new artificial intelligence tool<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/qgkDm2jRRpdeA_JvL7ImYIuGHwfToDG2kymUaGMyGMaCIrcRDnsxLUKE96_W_IIeNVqxpAXlMLNioUJZYybDOH5UivsMFR-TRfNVd6vlgWm9uCRnoz8bmZFuYNL7c618tRcFG4jM5bMWvnSlq5LgWaGrcsH_8nEuW1Wg0gKncshm1RDJrDqxrGxA5-nXnqcd1hlF1hMEq-A57nV1XLJi1DWuO2bPlvqVCTvNRd6USiwcBC5BS_IUgGOnCSZAwpbzlWSg-xX8G7UnKYfZzO0Sw-h-LR-UkSOtPY3DTI3vzBV-z2i2sg_789Iq1HI8RKO_evY1Rjcbjbt0cAxLSXbrhN80SCXTZrT1oNgBLwVcfORMr5r-1V30hCXChA/Nl1KZAHAqBl6zdv9I912gtZLeT1Ty6Eq/18>, people get nervous about the software business, and software stocks and bonds drop. The yields on loans to other software companies, companies that are similar to my borrower, go up by 0.5% over the course of the day. I call up my borrower to check in, and they say oh yeah, we saw that headline but were not too worried, everythings fine. How much is my asset  the companys note  worth? There is a conventional answer, which is about $98. [1] The price of a debt instrument moves inversely with interest rates; as the market demands higher interest rates from borrowers like my software company, the value of those companies existing debt goes down. If I sold my note for $98, the buyer would get a yield of 8.5%, which is the new market rate. The mark-to-market value of my note is $98. But I might object: Well, no, Im not going to sell my note for $98, or for any other price. Im just going to wait my five years, collect 8% interest along the way, and get $100 at the end. I thought that proposition was worth $100 yesterday, and I think its worth $100 today. Nothing has changed, with the asset, or the company, or me. Oh sure sure sure stuff in the outside markets has changed, and other people are more nervous about software credit. But I dont see how that affects me. I am not more nervous. Theyll probably change their minds tomorrow; it is nonsense to say that this loan was worth $100 yesterday and $98 today and for all I know $101 tomorrow. Itll pay $100 in five years with interest, its a perfectly good performing loan, its worth $100 until I have some objective reason to think that it isnt. [2] Probably a lot of you got very itchy reading that last paragraph, and I promise that I got very itchy writing it. But I want to argue that its not insane, and that which answer  $98 or $100  is correct depends on the purposes for which you are using the answer. Here are some purposes: 1. If I run a hedge fund, the right answer is $98, and it is very important that I mark this note to market in my accounting system. For one thing, just as a matter of intellectual rigor and market discipline, my job is to make money every day, and I need to know exactly what every asset is worth on the market so that I can make good trades. (If I am trading notes like this every day, it seems silly for me to say well I wont sell this one so its worth $100.) Also, a lot of outside people rely on my marks. I charge my investors a performance fee  20% of their gains or whatever  based on market returns, so I need to price everything using market prices. And I probably have a lot of leverage  I borrow a lot of money from banks, secured by my investments  and the banks are sure going to mark those assets to market. The banks are giving me margin loans against the value of my assets, and if that value goes down  measured by market prices  I will get margin calls. 2. If I run a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund, the right answer is $98, and mark-to-market accounting is again very important. Not, mostly, for the hedge funds reasons: I dont charge performance fees or, probably, borrow much. But because the investors in my mutual fund can get daily liquidity: Every day, they can take money out or put money in. They will do this at NAV: If they take money out, I will pay them the net asset value of their shares; if they put money in, I will sell them shares at the net asset value. If the net asset value of my fund does not reflect market prices, this will collapse: If my investors can take out $100 when their shares are only worth $98, then they will take out too much money and leave remaining investors with too little. Also, if the investors take out too much money, they can effectively force me to sell the note (to pay them back), so its value really has to be $98, the price I could sell it for today. 3. If I run a bank, I am a very special snowflake and generally am not supposed to mark loans to market in my financial statements. I loaned the company $100, nothing has changed, so thats worth $100 is the normal way that banks account for loans. The theory of a bank is that it can make loans and hold them to maturity, so it doesnt need to mark them up and down to reflect fluctuating markets. There is some complication and nuance to this, a lot of people dont like it, and it is not clear that it is really defensible anymore. But I also pointed out that there are various not-best-practices things here, and asking ChatGPT for legal advice is one of them. Not only in the sense that ChatGPT might get its legal advice wrong, but also in the sense that ChatGPT is not your lawyer and so your conversations with it are not privileged. The London-based startup is part of a cohort of ‘neoclouds’ - young companies responding to the huge uptick in demand for compute, triggered by the AI boom, by building data centres. title: FW: 12/03/26: Die Krise der Konsumfinanzierer, Wer den neuen Schufa-Score nutzt
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Thursday, 12 March 2026 06:15:27 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 12/03/26: Die Krise der Konsumfinanzierer, Wer den neuen Schufa-Score nutzt Außerdem: Girocard via iPhone  so viele Volksbank-Kunden sind aktiviert [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/57197114-2df1-d3d8-6586-607a05ca5755.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=df3d0bc732&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Krise der Konsumfinanzierer  jetzt bricht auch noch das Neugeschäft weg Im aktuellen Zahlenwerk der Santander Consumer Bank wimmelt es  wie diese Woche exklusiv berichtet<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=abfb102afd&e=8f69674dd2>  von Hiobsbotschaften. Da war die emporschießende Risikovorsorge. Der Einbruch des Provisionsgeschäfts (wegen der Regulierung der Restschuld-Versicherung). Und die Abschreibung auf die Hyundai Capital Bank Europe, also auf die Autofinanzierungs-Tochter mit dem Restwert-Kollaps<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=2e808216e0&e=8f69674dd2>. Den erstaunlichsten Befund allerdings hatten wir bei unserer Ad-hoc-Analyse sogar übersehen. So ist bei der Santander Consumer Bank auch noch die Neukreditvergabe gecrasht. Zumindest im sogenannten Direktgeschäft, also beim Vertrieb klassischer Ratenkredite. Der entsprechende Absatz belief sich im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr auf nur noch 1,5 Mrd. Euro  verglichen mit dem Vorjahr ein Einbruch um 29% (!). Vor allem der Filialvertrieb scheint dabei extrem unter Druck zu stehen: Trotz des immer noch recht dichten Filialnetzes (wobei sich das ja gerade ändert) generierte die deutsche Santander nur mehr einen stationären Absatz von rund 670 Mio. Euro, gemessen an bis zu 1,2 Mrd. Euro in manchen Vorjahren. Nun ist die Santander sicherlich ein Extrembeispiel. Tendenziell sieht es anderswo in der Branche allerdings genauso aus: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=a0dab5f8bd&e=8f69674dd2> Mehr zum Thema in unserem Archiv: * Exklusiv: Die Risikokosten der deutschen Santander haben sich verfünffacht (!). März 2026)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=235bef1a06&e=8f69674dd2> * Die DZ Bank hat jetzt wieder eine ausgewiesene Problemtochter  die Teambank. Februar 2026)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=5ee772fde4&e=8f69674dd2> * Exklusiv: Hier kommt die Roadmap für die Deutschland-Offensive der Creditplus-Mutter. FS Premium (23. April 2025)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=289cdca6ab&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/055d3feb-d58f-c3ea-7e48-6323dfd6b403.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=fe894af555&e=8f69674dd2> Wero ersetzt die girocard? Der digitale Euro wird alles dominieren? Die Debatte ist laut, meinungsstark - und wird in Teilen zu isoliert geführt. Doch wer sieht den Wald vor lauter Bäumen? Warum es nicht um Sieger, sondern um Rollen, Übergänge und Systemlogik geht, analysiert OSTHAVEN hier.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c2246371d1&e=8f69674dd2> Wie die deutsche "Basel"-Revolution in Europa zermahlen wurde (frei zugänglich) Als Finanz-Szene im letzten Sommer die "vertraulichen" Non-Paper zur Revision des Basel-Regimes öffentlich machte (siehe hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=4e00b90737&e=8f69674dd2> und hier<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ccb36a34fc&e=8f69674dd2>), da konnte mancher Bankvorstand nicht glauben, was er da las. Meinten Bundesbank und Bafin das wirklich ernst? Also dass, erstens, bei kleinen und mittelgroßen Banken die Kapitalgewichtung aufgehoben wird. Und dass, zweitens, bei größeren Banken das regulatorische Eigenkapital (also die CRR-Welt) vom regulatorischen Abwicklungskapital (also von der MREL-Welt) separiert wird. Die Vorschläge, ersonnen von Nikolas Speer (Leiter Bankenaufsicht bei der Bafin) und Karlheinz Walch (Leiter Bankenaufsicht bei der Bundesbank), hatten etwas Umstürzlerisches. Und selbstverständlich lösten sie eine lebhafte Diskussion aus, wobei die Fronten bisweilen einen lustigen Verlauf nahmen, etwa, als sich der deutsche Sparkassenverband für das angestrebte "Kleinbanken-Regime" aussprach (also für die Abschaffung der Kapitalgewichtung zugunsten der Leverage Ratio)  der hessische Sparkassenverband aber dagegen. Indes: So munter über das Thema auch gestritten wurde, irgendwie hatte man die ganze Zeit das Gefühl, einer Scheindebatte beizuwohnen, in die sich selbst die eingefleischtesten Lobbyisten allenfalls mit halber Kraft hineinwarfen. Weil: Ja, mochte schon sein, dass es Bundesbank und Bafin tatsächlich ernst war. Aber wem sonst noch? Also auf europäischer (und damit auf der entscheidenden) Ebene. Jedenfalls: Im Dezember hat die EZB ihren mit großer Spannung erwarteten HLTF-Bericht vorgelegt  das Kürzel steht für "High-Level Task Force (on Simplification)". Der Auftrag der zu Jahresbeginn aufgesetzten Arbeitsgruppe war, die europäische Bankenregulierung einer grundlegenden Überprüfung zu unterziehen, immer entlang des politisch formulierten Ziels, die Dinge, wo immer möglich, zu vereinfachen. 17 Reformvorschläge sind es letztlich geworden. Und, tja, was soll man sagen? Die revolutionären Einreichungen aus deutschen Landen finden sich in dem HLTF-Report nicht wirklich wieder. Unsere Analyse aus dem Dezember, jetzt für kurze Zeit vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (10 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=49def5d796&e=8f69674dd2> Heute im Premium-Newsletter * Exklusiv: Gegenüber Medien zog eine namhafte Genobank eine "positive Bilanz" ihres Geschäftsjahrs. Unsere Recherchen zeigen: In Wirklichkeit fiel ein Verlust an * Die Deutsche Bank wollte (angeblich) einen großen Abwickler von Lebensversicherungen übernehmen. Äh, und jetzt immer noch? * Welche Banken bereits den neuen Schufa-Score einsetzen (also den, der nur noch ein dutzend Bonitäts-Merkmale aufweist) * Wie viele Volksbank-Kunden bereits die neue Girocard-Lösung fürs iPhone nutzen (also den NFC-basierten Ansatz unter Umgehen von Apple Pay ...) Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/ff23bf10-d905-d852-0d1a-7d6e08bdd499.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=cfba959baa&e=8f69674dd2> Jetzt neu bei Finanz-Szene  unser Private-Banking-Letter: Was ist los bei Berenberg, Bethmann und Co.? Welche Pläne verfolgen Sparkassen und Volksbanken im Private Banking? Und was setzen Deutsche und Coba der Wealth-Management-Offensive der großen Auslandsbanken entgegen? Die Antworten gibt es künftig einmal monatlich in unserem Private-Banking-Letter. Stattdessen streben die Zentralbanker nun einen Umzug in die Innenstadt an. Die Kosten für die neue Immobilie sollen "deutlich" selbst unter jenen 1,6 Mrd. Euro liegen, mit denen zuletzt für eine stark abgespeckte "Campus"-Variante kalkuliert worden war. Kurz Die Nassauische Sparkasse, nach Bilanzsumme die Nummer elf im Sektor, hat ihren Zinsüberschuss im abgelaufenen Geschäftsjahr um 9% auf 281 Mio. Euro (= 1,85% der DBS) hochgedreht. Das Betriebsergebnis vor Bewertung stieg um 12% auf 144 Mio. Prediction market brokering The way the stock market works is that if a share of stock trades at $50, you can buy it for $50, and then if it goes up to $55 you can sell it for $55 and make a $5 profit. The way the market for crude oil works is different. If crude oil is trading at $95 per barrel, you cant really send your broker $95 and get back a barrel of oil. (Where would you put it?) Instead, the normal way to trade crude oil is with futures contracts: You buy a one-month futures contract now at $95, and if oil is trading at $92 or $107 in a month, you lose $3 or make $12, respectively. Someone else is on the other side of the contract: She sells you the contract now at $95, and if oil is trading at $92 or $107 in a month, she makes $3 or loses $12; her losses pay for your winnings and vice versa. I will loosely call this person your counterparty, though in fact both you and she deal with the commodities futures exchange and have no direct contact with each other. You could imagine a world in which you buy the contract now by paying $95, and at expiration you get back $92 or $107 or whatever. Or you could imagine a world in which no money changed hands at the beginning, and you and your counterparty just agreed that, in a month, youll pay her $1 for every $1 oil is below $95, and shell pay you $1 for every $1 oil is above $95, but no money will change hands between now and then. In fact the way commodities exchanges generally work is somewhere in between: You dont pay $95 at the beginning, but you dont pay zero either. You put down a deposit<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/K6iL08C9_Gs4bvZ9nhoAUI9ZCvd8UYTgTnZv-kyiXPxncU3jks_b7pMZv8m81dRWlv6uE5xLjj-7W6t9lUfrcK0_DhD5AqCDFGNYH-4JtR9vbHqb-RKCuwv-NElIpDJ0ycvWGjQ1ujz4x-RLcF4zqJr2bK-18Xij8XRKsQMcHo_o9E8eMNVD0XW3cVBvUwm_3zuF_Zx3YKIuYJAtSkFubcdeWKzov2Q1Xiy90ZCnfvmBsfie8nEscfV_umhgaxP-Psj7RkTORDoBNxMDo_TaFQuubgOn_aK-aYg9qnGMe1ySxiZjsDW9jG3HYTdtlFwFHXqDDlrOBuuS6-ckdji49zcYKuFF4dmSEFLuH4CM4eWdCWTorvRPKiMTng/m8eWRo_Jngv7iiRuAOlmeLpPsSJYMVVC/18>  margin  with the exchange, so the exchange knows youll be good for the money, and your counterparty also puts down a deposit (even though she is selling the contract). (The deposit is around $9<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/YsFHeVuxtVPGEf1LQM4VfpsWlQ-b6Rn6ZB8uVUdd7KAtgfkwepwlxGzjX7dm230pULUgfww4mlaxlujVbC6ByA30URjlQFKzJ3k4OHZsnCLIQiTUax2YirdjrmROh46Rf_HuskiFgm_R9rJu_2DQsGFSnLF9DomjPmTSG3zCgLR4w9aebyeo5WiPLdveXSsln1c6FqpDw20ku3JYpZnsW9r7QjOFjxtY0KKrQPdLFivN83c1kkw-ZTtUXiBIQxAQtP4tIt5yc-MDJVBLrWrd845Re8Ve5lXFaGBkdN_CSddMe6Au5c77gy3rXyogHOxey1PFgt_H-o22Cy7TSxelpQpm6RnEt439RdM4HSDcsClJEPOYkGncjhimBQ/GaCNOhvhpjVodA4Tgwo57B2mEpUcXzBs/18>.) And then as the price of oil moves around your margin will go up or down: If oil goes up, your counterparty will deposit more margin and youll take some back. So commodities futures provide leverage. If you are a big hedge fund who wants to bet on the price of oil, you can do that without tying up too much of your cash. You put up $9, you get exposure to $95 worth of crude oil, and if crude oil prices go up by 10% you roughly double your money. (If they go down 10% you lose your bet.) But leverage creates risk. The futures exchange (or, rather, the clearinghouse) has to set margin levels to cover potential market moves, and then it has to track prices and update margins  calling margin from people who have lost money, sending margin back to people who have made money  every day. There is a whole apparatus for making sure that losing bettors pay, so that winning bettors can get paid. We talk from time to time about this system, mostly when it breaks down. You might dislike this. You might say: No, this is dumb, everyone should put up all the money at the start, just like they do in the stock market. You pay $95, you get an oil contract, and then at the end you make or lose money, but nobody ever has to issue a margin call or post more money. There are two problems with that approach: 1. Hedge funds like leverage, this market is more efficient with leverage, blah blah blah. 2. The subtler problem is that this is impossible. The long side of a futures contract can just put up 100% of the money Day One, sure, no problem. But the short side cant. A futures contract is a bet between two people, one of whom bets that oil will go up and one of whom bets that it will go down. If you are long, you can put up $95, and if oil goes to zero you lose all your money and cant lose more. (Or can you?<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/XH0EGbIwBLoC4nRVqevIqs0zzIA-WgXHaJKRRJhBpMj0U_EbpDQ915W2bkdcJdhFfkgSnOCzQ400PwT3wZIWN7QWYRBSvu4_Cwk3E7JborSYaPvdwVBTle2ZA8CXR0cNbU-SV48XM47Qm_h9WdDXqVBJ5bK7gOL-sl-D67LAT9pdg-rIFCSYFfokEn-zPOdF7CFIHGQfbec5TvygfUexwon5A1hQ0XtrQpEXIZB0_BCS4xmYnUR6E3WbSLO25HOglVaXuHZSh5eY-NoOXFyql1P2mhvtcy6ZqS4g5x4v87CaFWTB0E-1iv_X1CvxWfSrlp91Mu84FupL22BOXty5NyaiiuGKa0vAqeFfzuUY2FeEJ6dWWyJF6N7Xp_c/yKwP_Zm0MHYmP_ZEtg6GwZCv0qD2sCsp/18>) But if you are short, you can put up $95, and if oil goes to $5,000 you have to pay much more money. Being short a financial contract is necessarily a leveraged trade. [1] You might still find this annoying. Okay, you say, I take the point that the short side of a commodities futures contract has unlimited risk. But we can fix that. Just chop off the tails. Make a new sort of oil futures contract with a price cap. I agree to buy oil at $95, and you agree to sell oil at $95, and if oil goes down to $40 I lose $55 and you make $55, and if oil goes up to $160 I make $65 and you lose $65. But: The contract is automatically capped at $190, twice the current price. [2] If oil goes to zero, I lose $95; if oil goes to $5,000, you only lose $95 (and I only make $95). We all know that going in, so I am not surprised or unhedged if oil really zooms up. And because our losses are capped, we can each put up $95 on Day One, and nobody ever needs to make margin calls or post more money or have any other sort of credit apparatus. My credit and your credit are completely taken out of the equation; we just put up all the money upfront. (Of course the exchange, or rather the clearinghouse, has to hang on to the money and give it back to the winner, but the exchange is not taking any leverage or market risk either, so as long as theyre not stealing the money its fine.) The advantage of this system is that it slims down the apparatus, and the risk, of the futures exchange. You dont need a big clearinghouse and complex margin rules; you dont need to vet exchange members to make sure theyre well capitalized, or require other traders to access the exchange through vetted members. The exchange can let anyone trade as long as they pay for their contracts up front. The exchange just needs a website and a bank account. The disadvantage is that hedge funds like leverage, blah blah blah, so this sort of entirely prepaid market will be less appealing to large levered professional investors. But it might be nice for retail traders who want to bet on oil. And you can solve the problem for the hedge funds. After all, the stock market loosely works this way  if you want to buy stock, you pay for it  and in fact hedge funds do lots of levered stock trades. They just borrow the money from their prime brokers: The stock exchange doesnt give you $50 of stock exposure for $5, but if youre a big hedge fund a bank will probably lend you $45 to buy $50 worth of stock. I realize that all of this sounds very eccentric, and I dont think I have ever seen anyone propose exactly this market structure, we should have futures exchanges but with 100% margins and capped moves in either direction. Except that this describes prediction markets. A prediction market is, in the US, a regulated commodities futures exchange, in which every futures contract pays out either exactly $1 or exactly $0. [3] If you are short a contract, the most you might have to pay is $1. If you are long, the most you might have to pay is $1. Therefore, prediction markets never need to think about margin: They can just sell a package of one long contract plus one short contract<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/k9rewBuq05kXpIBqFdlduBZ_PILc6j4v_wbcdbEWm0PPA275Rsq1g_NTnzU0p7YFQF1JjpH0p2zJbrStioJlXH_7_XrSwFxuHF9KGsJYiYjgdNf-yQodTr6r9UQziQhBdJGJNNgM_pcKZCAv-d9OW8HvbPIOP5gbEUAOP27afKamiZUIKOteVdN_b3fAhkUwhWG_iwcFLMgMhZ_SaNSBqpYQFf6qx94Bq5Y2pwf4Ea4ldEr-YDXB8QFpwxPAK2txTxuzNsCg_9F9kh2rs9eg1beSNXdHztcAK0byjltAokZD68IHStaTbRgvcLZBml98mf98GdAFmxJrkzUueVIep8QI7LQm7axH0ad2fHIL3mSHhWP06WNWxtZq6Lo/B5VY4u9rChi-cphMoPyhDImCoQP6aiff/18> for $1, and then theyll have the dollar, and then when the contracts mature theyll either give the dollar to the long or theyll give it to the short. [3] Or, in extremely rare cases (see the Death Markets section of this column lol), some intermediate amount in which the long and short sides still add up to $1. [4] Leverage is one, but there is also the opposite problem of *you* taking the *exchanges* (Kalshis) credit. Going through a clearing broker means that your exposure is to a familiar name, not a consumer website. title: Iran's Strait Closure Drives Oil Higher | Bloomberg Businessweek Daily 3/12/2026
content: On today's episode of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily, Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec speak with Bloomberg Economics chief geoeconomics analyst Jennie Welch on the impact on global energy markets as Iran's supreme leader says that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed. Then, Skyler Weinand, chief investment officer at Regan Capital, discusses market reaction to escalations in the conflict. Plus, Jason Greenblath, senior portfolio manager at American Century Investments, discusses the credit landscape as Amazon drives corporate bond sales to a record single-day high. Finally, Myles Miller gives an update on a shooting at synagogue in West Bloomfield, Michigan. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: FW: 13/03/26: Genos stinken gegen Apple Pay an, Updates zu SumUp und Bitpanda
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Friday, 13 March 2026 06:34:48 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 13/03/26: Genos stinken gegen Apple Pay an, Updates zu SumUp und Bitpanda Außerdem: Wieso Banken einen "digitalen Bebauungsplan" für ihre IT brauchen [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/7f3a766a-909d-8a0c-5794-11f4afaa96ad.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=56688e59f9&e=8f69674dd2> Wochen-Podcast (KW 11) "Vielleicht zeigen die Volksbanken, dass Apple Pay doch nicht so überdominant ist" [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/ad40a1a3-caec-61f7-66be-e857cd7a6d8f.jpg] Die Themen diesmal: #1: Deutsche Bank? Minus 5% (allein am Donnerstag). Wie und warum die Bankaktien jetzt doch abrauschen #2: Die Genossen feiern sich für 500.000 Aktivierungen bei der Girocard-Lösung fürs iPhone  womöglich zu Recht! #3: Warum es aus Nutzersicht convenient sein kann, wenn die Bezahlfunktion in die Banking-App integriert ist #4: Wir haben da mal eine Theorie!!! Warum Cashback-Services (also: Geldabheben an der Kasse) immer noch so wenig genutzt werden #5: Der Einbruch des Neugeschäfts in der Konsumfinanzierung: Was davon ist Konjunktur, was ist digitale Konkurrenz? #6: Der Wert billiger Einlagen zeigt sich dieser Tage bei den VR-Banken  und erstaunlicherweise auch im Coba/Unicredit-Poker #7: Eine (zumindest gefühlte) Lehre der Bilanzsaison: Die Sparkassen legen mehr Innovationstempo an den Tag als die Genossen #8: Das neue Jugendkonto der Volksbanken  auf welche Features stehen eigentlich junge Kunden? Auf geht's: Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=a5872d0242&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/ad59069d-e637-aa50-e3ca-6d405b0c9c2e.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e853c7c3f9&e=8f69674dd2> Starten Sie mit frischen KI-Impulsen in Ihre Kaffeepause. Die AI Coffee Break bietet Ihnen in nur 45 Minuten kompakte Einblicke zu aktuellen KI-Trends und praxisnahen Anwendungen. Einfach, inspirierend und interaktiv  die perfekte Mischung für Ihre nächste Tasse Kaffee. Jetzt anmelden!<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=4e5098109c&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Topverdiener der Deutschen Bank erhält >18 Mio. Euro  während die Aktie crasht: Ausgerechnet am Tag der Veröffentlichung ihres Vergütungsberichts hat die Deutsche Bank einen der aufreibendsten Handelstage der letzten Jahre erlebt. Nach einer stundenlangen Abwärtsfahrt notierte die Aktie des größten hiesigen Geldinstituts am Nachmittag um bis zu 7,4% im Minus  erst kurz vor dem regulären Handelsschluss erholten sich die Papiere etwas und beendeten den Tag schließlich bei 25,70 Euro (5,3%). Seit Jahresbeginn hat die DBK-Aktie jetzt 24% verloren und damit deutlich mehr als die Commerzbank (17%), die auch am Donnerstag etwas glimpflicher davonkam als der Lokalrivale und zum Handelsende bei 30,23 Euro notierte (4,1%). Etwas in den Hintergrund rückte, was sich Spannendes im Geschäfts- und Vergütungsbericht verbarg. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=dfd4416cad&e=8f69674dd2> News * Die Capital Group hat ihre Beteiligung an der Deutschen Bank reduziert: Wie aus einer am späten Donnerstag veröffentlichten Pflichtmitteilung hervorgeht, hält der US-Asset-Manager nunmehr noch 2,9% an der Großbank nach zuletzt gemeldeten 4,9% im August 2025. Mutmaßlich fiel bei der Reduktion ein hübscher Gewinn an  der Aufbau der Position zwischen April 2024 und Januar 2025 erfolgte noch zu Kursen zwischen 14 und 18 Euro versus aktuell knapp 26 Euro. * Das deutsch-britische Payment-Fintech SumUp kommt dem angestrebten Börsengang möglicherweise näher. Wie "Bloomberg" (Paywall)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=44a6a3ac2a&e=8f69674dd2> berichtet, soll der Zahlungsterminal-Spezialist verschiedene Investmentbanken wegen eines etwaigen IPOs in Europa angesprochen haben  nachdem es zuletzt noch hieß, SumUp präferiere ein US-Listing. Im Raum stehe eine Bewertung "von 10 Mrd. Dollar oder mehr" (also merklich weniger als die 15 Mrd. Dollar, die im letzten Sommer diskutiert wurden). * Der auch hierzulande weitverbreitete österreichische Krypto-Broker Bitpanda vermeldet für das abgelaufene Geschäftsjahr einen "bereinigten Umsatz" (ausgeklammert wurden unter anderem die sonstigen betrieblichen Erträge) von 371 Mio. Euro, verglichen mit dem Vorjahr eine Steigerung um 16%. Darüber hinaus ist von einem ebenfalls "bereinigten" Ebitda von 13 Mio. Euro die Rede (7%). The newsletter’s completely free, just like Alphaville<https://substack.com/redirect/3f2e8b22-d3e1-4d2b-8ac6-34293a2abd4a?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. All the commonly cited benchmarks are futures, of which there’s never a shortage, so high and low bids are just bets on the likelihood of delivery. Price volatility is a measure of how difficult it is at any given moment to suppress the knowledge that no one knows anything. Here's this week’s view. We made the chart below on Thursday afternoon, so by publication time today it’s likely to be missing at least four tape bombs: [https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!iR6r!,w_1100,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F08904be0-960a-4850-be4c-00d3025fbe88_1200x1200.png]<https://substack.com/redirect/3b0f54de-acb3-406d-903f-93a6a65e6aea?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> Lots of noise, not much signal. Wild price moves<https://substack.com/redirect/e30603f9-4160-4204-bf51-ce7c90124dd0?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> reflect uncertainty while telling us absolutely nothing about when tankers might dock, how soon jets could be grounded, and if Thailanders can use elevators again<https://substack.com/redirect/5c250b54-f1fd-4e9d-882a-e93ce0094199?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Our perspectives on where crude demand meets supply are always by degrees of separation. This relationship between physical and paper oil is the subject of a newsletter by University of Lausanne professor Gianluca Benigno<https://substack.com/redirect/6a166454-7449-4b41-a61b-be5088eefaa8?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Prompted by reports that the US Treasury wants to combat price spikes by shorting oil futures<https://substack.com/redirect/43478fcd-0011-475a-8e7a-f59986ac99cd?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, Benigno explains that contract pricing hangs on confidence about delivery. Dependable supply is the only way to underpin that confidence. And while suppressing front-end futures prices could reduce the incentive to hoard, the only hoarding that happens during an oil shock is for need, not greed; each useful barrel “begins to trade less like a commodity and more like insurance”, he says. Meanwhile, over at Reuters, columnist Clyde Russell highlights that cash-settled Dubai cargoes are trading at a wide premium to the equivalent swaps<https://substack.com/redirect/eceaa806-df80-4ac0-bcca-aab425fd8563?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Paper traders are more confident than oil consumers about a quick ceasefire and manageable supply disruptions, which “seems untethered from the reality on the ground”, Russell says. To argue that a market is clearing at the wrong price is never not brave, but that’s particularly true when prices are moving like angry wasps in a Sodastream. In more predictable times, owning an oil future can be a hedge or a guarantee, whereas owning a barrel of crude before it’s needed is always a huge pain in the ass<https://substack.com/redirect/a61f9d02-7bd8-48db-8b2b-4372cf37ca19?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Premiums now being paid at the dock might be no more than a consequence of unpredictable times. There’s lots more to read on the theme but, honestly, unless you’re a Vitol trader or own a Lego factory, it’s OK not to bother. Commodity products are valued by what the buyer wants them for today, on known knowns. Those trying to guess what buyers will want tomorrow, on unknown unknowns, are asking for trouble. Of the two-dozen or so 2026 investment bank and fund manager outlooks<https://substack.com/redirect/182cf00b-6149-4053-b4f0-bea2aa9b8765?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4> we collected in December, only a couple make passing reference to Iran, and none contain the word “Hormuz”. All of their forecasts are for crude to end the year gently up or range-bound. Don't get us wrong. Whether oil costs $60 or $120 a barrel is very important. But to the average person, whether first-month futures were $60 or $120 a barrel this morning is really only important for setting inflation expectations<https://substack.com/redirect/5c870f22-103b-43c4-82bd-d113ed31315f?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>, which is what makes the Treasury plan to short them slightly less silly, though it’s still very very silly<https://substack.com/redirect/fe2376c1-7416-446e-9be1-a1f4505ace83?j=eyJ1IjoicDBzaDEifQ.aWeIhmNCVGNColYUmI1TE7JzeHpAMb4ONxSzBHYhJl4>. Fuel price dependent, the money could be better spent on hiring skywriters to write “no one knows anything” in big letters each day over our major financial centres. title: FW: 16/03/26: Der Masterplan der deutschen Santander, Scalable kommt mit Kampfzins
content: ________________________________ From: Finanz-Szene  Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de> Sent: Monday, 16 March 2026 06:15:39 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com> Subject: 16/03/26: Der Masterplan der deutschen Santander, Scalable kommt mit Kampfzins Außerdem: Zwei Updates zu N26, Neuer Fintech-CEO, Promi-Abgang bei Dt. Bank [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png] Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/8f98afd5-5655-b2b8-4989-eb7a1ee46dc7.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=8d17ee4138&e=8f69674dd2> Exklusiv: Der Masterplan, wie die Santander Consumer Bank aus der Krise kommen will Liebe Leserinnen und Leser, hängt Ihnen unsere ausufernde Berichterstattung zur Santander Consumer Bank so langsam zum Hals heraus? Ha! Fragen Sie uns mal!! Uns kommt sie sogar schon zu den Ohren raus!!! Denn wir müssen's ja recherchieren, Sie dagegen brauchen es nur zu lesen bzw. haben sogar die Freiheit, einfach weiterzuscrollen, zum Beispiel genau jetzt, in diesem Moment, scroooollllll ... Wiewohl: Genau das wollen wir Ihnen ehrlicherweise dann doch nicht empfehlen. Denn spannend oder wenigstens relevant ist ja doch, was da gerade in Mönchengladbach passiert, zumindest im Sinne einer Case Study: Da gerät eine über viele Jahre lang notorisch erfolgreiche und scheinbar bestens aufgestellte Kreditbank urplötzlich in Schwierigkeiten, und so richtig weiß man eigentlich gar nicht, wie das passiert ist. Okay, ein paar Indizien gab es. Da war die große Restrukturierung 2024/25<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=27cbca83b2&e=8f69674dd2> (wobei, restrukturieren tut so eine Auslandsbank ja eigentlich immer, auch wenn es gut läuft). Da war der etwas unvermittelte CEO-Austausch<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=a774a2d833&e=8f69674dd2> (wobei, auch ein Wechsel des Vorstandschefs weist ja nicht zwingend auf Probleme hin, zumal der alte in diesem Fall auch nicht mehr ganz jung war). Und dann waren da vor ein paar Wochen die Berichte über weitere Filialschließungen<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=e81d13023c&e=8f69674dd2>. Plus: Letzten Montag legten wir von Finanz-Szene dann ja offen, dass die Santander Consumer Bank in den letzten Jahren deutlich an Ergebnis eingebüßt hat<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=778772d510&e=8f69674dd2>. Die Sache ist aber nun, dass die Lage insbesondere im Filialengeschäft sogar noch düsterer zu sein scheint, als wir es letzte Woche geschrieben hatten. So jedenfalls liest sich ein uns vorliegendes internes Dokument. Was sich in besagten Dokumenten allerdings ebenfalls findet, das ist der strategische Masterplan, wie die deutsche Santander wieder in die Vorhand kommen will. Alles weitere hier (inklusive einer großen Deutschland-Karte, welche Filialen schließen): FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=38cc213f26&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/974e1eb4-f62b-12f5-2bdf-07d4ba25f856.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=04ec4f59b4&e=8f69674dd2> AI stellt alles in Frage  In Fabriken sind fast alle Arbeitsschritte auf Maschinen und Roboter übergegangen. Jetzt stehen Bürotätigkeiten vor der Ablösung, denn AI kann viele kognitive Aufgaben ersetzen. Ein spannender Prozess bezüglich Arbeit und der Rolle des Menschen startet. Wie Agentic AI zum strategischen Wettbewerbsvorteil eingesetzt werden kann, zeigt unser Whitepaper. Jetzt downloaden<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=d76998a4ba&e=8f69674dd2> Briefing Exklusiv: Scalable geht mit Tagesgeld-Konto nächsten Schritt gen Banking. Das Münchner Investment-Fintech Scalable Capital kommt erstmals mit einem klassischen Bankprodukt an den Markt. Laut Informationen von Finanz-Szene wird der Neobroker zeitnah ein eigenes Tagesgeldkonto launchen, nicht nur in Deutschland, sondern auch in weiteren europäischen Ländern. Der Zinssatz liegt zum Start bei 2,5% (für Neu- wie Bestandskunden gleichermaßen und bei unbegrenzter Einlagenhöhe)  eine ziemliche Kampfansage! Dazu muss man wissen, dass Scalable seinen Brokerage-Kunden für deren Liquidität auch jetzt schon eine Verzinsung in Höhe des EZB-Einlagenzinses (also 2,0%) zahlt. Rein inhaltlich stellt das eigene Tagesgeldkonto also eine begrenzte Weiterentwicklung der Produktpalette dar. Gleichwohl geben die Münchner sechs Monate nach dem Erhalt der Bafin-Lizenz erstmals konkret zu erkennen, sich stärker gen Bankgeschäft zu orientieren. Dabei behält sich Scalable vor, die Einlagen auf die eigene Bilanz zu nehmen oder sie mittels Treuhand-Sammelkonten an eine der Partnerbanken (Deutsche Bank, HSBC, J.P. Morgan) bzw. an einen Geldmarktfonds weiterzureichen. Blog Exklusiv: IKB vollzieht radikalen Strategieschwenk im Kreditgeschäft. Seit Jahren läuft bei der IKB eine bilanzielle Groß-Operation, die darauf hinausläuft, die ursprünglich offenbar immensen Risiken im Wertpapierportfolio zu reduzieren  und den dabei entstehenden Aufwand durch die Auflösung von Reserven aus dem Fonds für allgemeine Bankrisiken zu kompensieren (siehe schon vor drei Jahren unsere Analyse > Ist die IKB ein Opfer ihrer Bilanz  oder ihrer Bilanzierung?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=409e324a2c&e=8f69674dd2>). Was dabei etwas in den Hintergrund gerät: 1.) Der Düsseldorfer Mittelstandsfinanzierer ist bei seinen Reinigungsarbeiten inzwischen offenbar soweit vorangekommen, dass sich der Eigentümer Lone Star jetzt eine krasse Ausschüttung in Höhe von 195 Mio. Euro (fast 700% des operativen Ergebnisses) genehmigen darf. Und 2.) Jenseits der Bilanz-OP tun sich bei der IKB aktuell auch im operativen Geschäft ein paar ziemlich bemerkenswerte Dinge. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=d965be27d8&e=8f69674dd2> Ticker * Dass die Hypo-Vereinsbank im vergangenen Jahr krasse 3 Mrd. Euro verdient hat  das war ja schon bekannt. Neu ist, an welchen Schrauben sie dabei dreht, insbesondere im Retailgeschäft. Unser Großbanken-Ticker: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=54a7a29709&e=8f69674dd2> * Firmenkunden-Topshot Jan-Philipp Gillmann verlässt die Deutsche Bank. Weitere prominente Abgänge bei großen deutschen Banken sowie einen CEO-Wechsel bei einem Berliner Fintech gibt's in unserem Personalien-Ticker: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=966c98b3f3&e=8f69674dd2> Anzeige [https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/a3ed8a3e-4268-96f1-c689-9051fa2c2108.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=003f78ae7d&e=8f69674dd2> Grenzüberschreitende Zahlungen sollten nicht dem Zufall überlassen sein. Wenn Zahlungen genau dann ankommen, wann sie sollen, entsteht Vertrauen. Visa Direct hilft, zuverlässig zu liefern. Mehr auf der Visa-Website erfahren<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=3d67007a00&e=8f69674dd2> News * Bei der Berliner Neobank N26 ist nach monatelangem Hickhack endlich die umstrittene neue Gesellschaftervereinbarung unterschrieben worden. Im Kern ging es bei der Auseinandersetzung darum, dass Valentin Stalf und Max Tayenthal (also die beiden Gründer, die sich letztes Jahr aus der operativen Führung zurückgezogen haben, aber immer noch rund 20% halten) auf ihre ursprünglich festgeschriebenen Sonderrechte als Co-Founder verzichten  während umgekehrt einige Großinvestoren ihre bei der letzten großen Finanzierungsrunde zugesagte Garantiedividende aufgeben. Zudem soll der Aufsichtsrat von sechs auf acht Mitglieder erweitert werden. Unklar ist weiterhin, ob auch Stalf selbst in das Kontrollgremium einzieht. Handelsblatt (Paywall)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=1f54537604&e=8f69674dd2> Kurz * Die französische Payone-Mutter Worldline hat eine Kapitalerhöhung über 392 Mio. Euro gestartet  mit der Folge, dass der Aktienkurs am Freitag um gut 4% einknickte (weil der Börsenwert vor der Erhöhung gerade mal noch rund 125 Mio. Euro betragen hatte). * Bei der vom BVR als "Präventions-Institut" geführten<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=73fd1edcc4&e=8f69674dd2> VR Plus Altmark-Wendland bahnt sich laut der lokalen "Elbe-Jeetzel-Zeitung" (Print) möglicherweise eine Abspaltung des Warengeschäfts von der eigentlichen Bank an  einzelne Bereiche sollen bereits verkauft worden sein. * Zu N26 haben wir auch noch einen Datenpunkt: Knapp zwei Monate nach dem Launch des "Kids Konto" verzeichnet die Neobank rund 7.000 Aktivierungen. Favoriten 1. Podcast (#203): Vielleicht zeigen die Volksbanken, dass Apple Pay doch nicht so überdominant ist. Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=cf9686cb6e&e=8f69674dd2> 2. Mögliche Cum-Ex-Wende: Crédit Agricole könnte >400 Mio. Euro zurückerhalten. FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=5b0ecbf8f1&e=8f69674dd2> 3. Topverdiener der Deutschen Bank erhält >18 Mio. Euro  während die Aktie crasht. FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=a9b3ca44da&e=8f69674dd2> 4. In Hessen bahnt sich die nächste Volksbanken-Fusion an. FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0f784fadbc&e=8f69674dd2> 5. by Martin Coulter

Good morning Luca,



Over the past week or so, a curious new phrase has been bouncing around the UK startup scene: “Londonmaxxing.”



The idea, popularised by a handful of influencers in and around the industry, is simple. If you want to maximise your chances of building a successful startup, get to London! Spend enough time bobbing around Soho cafes and Shoreditch coworking spaces and, before long, you'll collide with the cofounder, investor or engineer who changes your trajectory.



After years of tech bros dismissing the capital as a crime-ridden hellhole and dreaming of relocating to Dubai, the sudden enthusiasm for London feels like a big U-turn. A combination of spring sunshine, blockbuster funding rounds and buzzy AI meetups has prompted some in the ecosystem to rediscover the city's virtues.



But the recent excitement also raises a question: what exactly is new here?



London has long been Europe’s deepest pool of VC money and entrepreneurial talent, giving rise to fintech giants like Revolut and helping nurture a growing cluster of AI startups.

Hélène Huby, founder and CEO of spacetech startup The Exploration Company, is not afraid to take risks — or fail.



Her company, which is only five years old, builds reusable and refillable vehicles to carry cargo to and from space stations in low-Earth orbit — and beyond.



It’s already (semi-) successfully sent cargo into space — and back — at a fraction of the cost, and time, achieved by other companies.

title: New World’s Top Shareholder Seeks to Refinance $932 Million Loan
content: Chow Tai Fook Enterprises Ltd., the main investment arm of Hong Kong billionaire Henry Cheng’s family, is looking to refinance an around HK$7.3 billion ($932 million) loan due in June, according to people familiar with the matter, testing banks’ appetite for exposure to a firm tied to the clan’s troubled property business.

title: UniCredit Makes €35 Billion Commerzbank Bid to Cross 30% Threshold
content: UniCredit made a €35 billion ($40 billion) bid for Commerzbank that will allow it to increase its shareholding beyond 30%, easing the path for a potential future acquisition. Bloomberg's Tommaso Ebhardt reports. (Source: Bloomberg)

content: UniCredit launched a voluntary takeover offer for Commerzbank on Monday.

title: BofA’s Mensah Sees ‘Healthy Cleanup’ in Private Markets
content: Bernard Mensah, who leads Bank of America Corp.’s international operations, says signs of strain in parts of the private credit market present an opportunity for “a very good, healthy cleanup.” Speaking on Bloomberg Television, Mensah adds: “It’ll shine a light on it. It will force people to look at their positions.”

title: German Government Rejects UniCredit Takeover Bid for Commerzbank
content: Germany’s conservative-led government dismissed a potential hostile takeover of Commerzbank AG by UniCredit SpA as “unacceptable” after the Italian lender made a €35 billion ($40 billion) bid for the Frankfurt-based bank.

title: Musk’s xAI Hiring Credit Experts, Bankers to Teach Grok Finance
content: Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence startup xAI is looking to hire bankers and private credit lenders to make its Grok chatbot better at finance strategy, joining rival AI firms in pushing software for investing professionals.

title: Private Credit Strain Is a ‘Healthy Cleanup’, BofA’s Mensah Says
content: Signs of strain in parts of the private credit market present an opportunity for “a very good, healthy cleanup,” according to Bernard Mensah, who leads Bank of America Corp.’s international operations.

New prediction market manipulation

In theory, a thing that you could do is:

  1.  Buy some short-dated out-of-the-money call options on a public company.
  2.  Call up a deals reporter at a prominent news outlet and say hey I hear Amalgamated Amalgamators is going to acquire Consolidated Widgets at $50 per share, you should publish that, its a big scoop, you will get a lot of clicks and keep your readers informed and win various journalism prizes.
  3.  The reporter is like thanks Ill look into it.
  4.  Time passes and the reporter does not publish the story you want.
  5.  So you call her back and say hey this Consolidated Widgets deal is really heating up, if you want to be first with the scoop youd better publish right now, you need to help the market understand this news.
  6.  The reporter is like yeah I called around and theres nothing to this rumor, sorry! [1]
  7.  You say no youre wrong, I promise, its real.
  8.  She says okay thanks for your input, Im going to hang up now.
  9.  You say Wait! If you publish the story I will pay you $10,000.
  10. She says What? No. Goodbye.
  11. You say Wait! If you dont publish the story I will kill your family.

There are, obviously, a lot of things wrong with this sequence of events. For one thing, you are trying to do market manipulation; you are trying to push up the price of Consolidated Widgets stock based on false information, which is illegal. Also the bribery and death threats are bad.

I just want to make the narrow point that, in theory, this could maybe work. That is, the published work of journalists can, sometimes, have a big effect on the prices of financial assets; in some cases, one journalist publishing one discrete factual statement can materially move the price of a stock and make a lot of money for people on one side of a trade, regardless of the underlying truth of the statement. News publications can serve, in effect, as oracles for the prices of financial assets, at least temporarily. And so if you could influence the right journalist in the right situation, with tricks or bribes or threats or whatever, then you could make a lot of money. Not illegal advice!

(Not me, though; Im never going to break merger news so please dont try to bribe or threaten me.)

On the other hand, this only maybe works, and only for a little while. News reports are not actually oracles for financial prices; the terms of stocks and bonds and options and futures do not generally refer to news reports for their resolution. [2]  A journalist reports Consolidated Widgets is in play, maybe its stock goes up briefly, it announces no were not, its stock goes down, never mind. [3]

One interesting fact about the rise of prediction markets is that they offer financial contracts that pay off on the occurrence of all sorts of real-world events, and if you are betting on all sorts of real-world events you need all sorts of sources of truth, and if you are looking for a general-purpose source of truth about arbitrary noteworthy facts, your natural inclination might be is it in the newspaper? And so journalists stories are, often, the actual official oracles for various prediction contracts. We have, for instance, talked<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/MFrWeotF8G822MvYu9sNjamg79dPqmK7xb6jTAOXbBpobQH2Iylefc2vckzOKRBKZZKDVsWF4bb_q455mVL0sOgyWjyaahWo2DfZ5Qwl9fnpkPcV1WCQ3RudQkltG7eZoxAtwSx8vzLmxCCXD6yUxPrln-izbmw_znRWogqrPVeJ3bZg-RwciPbfd5uSZNsMlYEKcdBjPaRhQbiEAvRUFMoj15KY-DRaw--t2oyHaW6lSv33M04JJC2d6VtfEVCiEv2ycagJw_g_6z6Pbrnnxc8G9_YAXkk3sfOlZ6X1i5Anf_K3uGDM64DMDoRZpD9ppWW-QZDlOG_98qv_APyh8hBZEDmWbKspjnHSiCJs9S5Sv71Kc3G9LX1McA/9cdPfebxpwPpnYUfEm-wNEvC8_oeef9A/18> a few times<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/LOl_u_2R5DFNzOkW4Fko5jJjZ9D5pezqKMLZR5VThnYtIwLFpmd9S-IaxgvJ-qssFF0j4tgwxAtUkCBUskVqtFMG29coob1fm0MvuUQtuhBuynoTXWnofqWny6bs_bfoZNMC6gS8nwGkxvnq8pixbNPiFiXV2C2Z23Nj9urcgYEJHcc0Y5wPAfWJhqvBO19rGOJ8Wnh2WvxgNNMjYlGOKHhKTVw3ZcHzDj9S_QeII0jOEkjvBiADjPWLq5LQskGjxvzyLIbRwQpLX-hBcWak9Tpx7tuacmuK33SyvWezYGleYqPLmeaE30KnaGj0dbzx4iM4r1iHdFJN6Vd9Urf1RXUN6A7T1xZWFPuWILUilhio1ySlvbsNwVkpWQ/NqItJfDxl9QdRvxNpSLYRQxeyIuF6LWV/18> about the Ali Khamenei out as Supreme Leader contracts<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-5uEnY5G-uB0b_AmL63wx9WDY1V_x4ZmJTWcgS-bz9WRwEErPmljM_A4Ri6ZOQ4gIlz7TpE3QtW8y-XIggWpHivOm5LoKaBeH9qkMDscYAUuzrcftbnajXHb2sz1YrN8XKDs1bovYWGqV3C7Q1guHEIJVPVJjfTOeDjwT_31_suWRZ7RI6SQDeh6q0-XGUqILQhYD2Ga6fuSih8yEc5Upw1BXX83fUNF1SnlS5olW-1DG5EPulbf9oosSeXlWqMCjDfvKsyWjLQopOzLrAKpULrNzsCsbWkpQORNqQkRkEFup_YCWEGVKTb_HPWAKOlIDNap3hCzWRnWlF1U-fvsFf5eCfcgaAhYE8_FB3giqZdI2NOyLOZtxoCwoPA/oOQ_IS64uIJ6IwFMksR4ly7q9w27Detm/18> on Kalshi. Those resolve based on reports from The New York Times, the Associated Press, Reuters, Axios, Politico, Semafor, The Information, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, MSNBC, and Ali Khamenei. If you could plant a few stories youd be in business.

I suppose one set of questions you might have is, like, what does this mean for the accuracy and information content and fairness and manipulability of prediction markets? And then another set of questions you might have is, what does this mean for journalists? A lot more opportunities to take bribes, but also a lot more chances to get death threats, and also more prosaically a lot of people emailing you politely but insistently to ask you to change your stories to make their bets pay off.

Anyway heres a Times of Israel story by Emanuel Fabian with the title Gamblers trying to win a bet on Polymarket are vowing to kill me if I dont rewrite an Iran missile story<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/VFMGfUoy6u8TAHoZepaqUNhf-dZ_J7OSTPYRC_1O1_uY45oS-E-hhT_kdvP6d2eg_LTckup5nj1d4UN7aQ7ajzXI39dQ1O7zOngJyLCqRE1UTD7enlMGBrcN5-aag_xUr1PFw3SFjzDeR5-dNjaWikElGiZpniawDwCqPjwNjHwwfqmUuxlg5nN6lGTHv0xNgUObn8YdZjBHg_j_-CB2LmwS7gMNQ-16e3e0a-Th6uZuAU96sZesiYLnU0o99BK9_s4aHn55kD3xnY8QxbLiw_cStK_MUnjadQwtelHdkh0yWKmUgdab5sasSqxhoBxX5JFVNdTj45xGeApCg73WgP4TLmjeo_zJoJgZ0IJl4Ffy_CXZLztNEJhkb7k/fLMuDlIOcusuUTOV1mxJ3Z-tEQFb4cfX/18>, and thats pretty much what its about, but as a journalist I definitely recognized the more mundane polite correction requests at the beginning:

Regarding your Times of Israel report that described todays launch as an impact  Beit Shemesh Municipality and MDA (Magen David Adom) later corrected their reports to clarify that what fell was an interceptor fragment, not a full missile, [one reader] claimed.

Id appreciate it if you could update your article, as in its current form it does not reflect reality. Alternatively, if you have information that it was indeed a full missile that was not intercepted, I would be glad to be corrected.

Eventually, though, bribes and death threats:

You have no idea how much youve put yourself at risk. Today is the most significant day of your career. You have two choices: either believe that we have the capabilities, and after you make us lose $900,000 we will invest no less than that to finish you. Or end this with money in your pocket, and also earn back the life you had until now. ...

If you decide to go with your ego and not with your head, you are leaving behind dozens of wealthy people from all over the world who will know that you performed market manipulation and stole from them. They know who you are, you dont know who they are. It took them less than 5 minutes to find out exactly where you live  how often you see your lovely parents  and exactly who your  brothers and sisters are.

Nuns

The way American shareholder democracy works is that, if you dont like something that a US public company is doing, you can buy some of its stock and demand that it make changes. The simplest way to do that is to buy one share and then call the investor relations number to register your complaint; this probably wont accomplish anything, but it might, and maybe it will make you feel better. [4]

The most effective way to do it is to buy 5% of the stock, submit your own nominees for the board, run a proxy contest, persuade other shareholders to vote for your slate, win<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/_LpCoRQP1Vt0UxKHnSFFvEQjGU7qavurRMo3oThbYuTic3GVbMb9AjIyK1G58XNfdie5n_9Awiw9lzoYMA3vyiEErwMrSChSXGXAwlJs52v6BfLFDSingTEUxIpfPSFbXvyYGnpNp5KpFt7t2QwPOr3lpJ0BnmbfMGSJehk9eBRKCN_gIWkh6OC9naJ6Bn3dF0qv0XXx0Aa3GKAMVo1SI_gP_9uH2f49LwPc33o0Waje_0PfltZfYCOfsjPebMFCyW-Ad3jwwWNTbOxMXp0BtosnZKkNwZ8Ov9F52gTID8VRyjsVGvWPa7LttlhiM0nFSODQCC-UPasj0yA3mkQvuEA9RRw9vSKwEgfjgW3la653_MAsdLdRZ-xvIkk/vgZp00ea9dtppOupRcXqKYV1ujRmWJcB/18>, replace the board, and run the company the way you want. This has a much higher degree of difficulty and is much more expensive, but if you have billions of dollars it is far more effective than the other approaches. Carl Icahn once launched a proxy fight<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/j-fnZnft-eypcdLoO_lM33J0mhK-XFTbuecCqRzxWn5KvwHbSLGksWKGUnR0YibvMECWP08AClPYSVVozTrDWT4cpNnwWko2-bs1gF_OXdVncMcOjiMdIGalYcEfiCsCW7dTUGA1Jp_bSRhl6Q8i9JLSVcHvlNYDiH98PnHP10nMgSyd2L-2Com5r7Y7xO0WRVMn6HR462E4n7_-eJTe9kAiAh1IQomnrDn3wett9fc9cXVJMqvZyiCSDjFmxpiH7EXKqIwIzCAZrHw9LiXFslTJhe-JJlZNXkfDUR17DAvoDZ_fcyUx0qZKVBE2peHP8k7b-3W6p3ZZoANKmZdNRM_oBJMmn5KBSPYQgKAz-4gKatQ3HI5yIcdCIH4/fMO1h5q-R_9c4vq_bvQkmfnx6Ng0zyzb/18> at McDonalds Corp. to get them to change their treatment of pigs. A variation on this is doing a hostile takeover, where you buy 100% of the stock and then really run the company however you want. There is an intermediate approach. You can buy at least $2,000 worth of stock, hold it for a while, and then submit a shareholder proposal for the companys annual meeting. This does not, I have to say, work very well. There are somewhat complex rules<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/MLzjhHxBaRbPXitp_eO1YWuXbMYh5qTHiy8W9VZ-av0QMVJoPCJKH1M9Bs26zALkqsiIAok9wQx-dp3X4s622Q_ndWYrkdgVe4GyvA-mOCpNJIDNxXhtYDhJqGkPblzOWnUnX2zWgD4mU8EHy5dhXiE93Jr-owtOMAIvE8EyQC4jv2yXOIA9ByNn7lr1E9fvFQPh_hNtkuMSG2OasBT7jjQYQDNaKNlPDGWnzd9GV0M-bZ1evko6pHPacyUHF7ZIoNJJCtf25yOUqZVh8dQJGS_c7O65d3ZzD_-VwH58WovzzcM4mB8oNbb7bhqOPgQJAIyhF2Yyva-ul00HfQ23IbJn5qBG1RYF8jXZ5J9y1LsaL4WY_zM4VqJgEIw/gf-4Gih8Z6x_axCIh27hhJg2ShC0_1an/18> for submitting shareholder proposals, and if you mess them up the company might be able to keep your proposal off the ballot. The rules significantly limit what your proposal can be about; if your proposal is, like, Resolved, this companys snack foods tasted better before you changed the recipe, please change it back, or Resolved, I bought a shirt from one of your stores and a button was missing and the sales clerk wouldnt give me a refund, please give me a refund, there is really no way to get it on the ballot and youre better off calling IR. In practice, these proposals tend to be about broad social and environmental issues  the company should be more (or less) diverse, it should pollute less (or more), etc.  or about the companys governance structure (its whole board should be up for election each year, its CEO should not also be the chair of the board, etc.), not about the details of the business. Also, the rules generally require that your proposal be non-binding: Even if you get it on the ballot, and even if a majority of shareholders vote for it, management still doesnt have to do anything about it.

This approach is far more complicated and time-consuming than calling investor relations, and far less effective than running a proxy fight, and in practice it seems to be mostly the domain of hobbyists and nuns. For the reasons laid out above, I dont think that this would have much of an impact on how public companies operate, but it would annoy the nuns. Federal regulators are looking at new rules that could rein in shareholders who hold as little as $2,000 in stock to get their proposals on proxy ballots. Business groups are pressing for higher ownership thresholds like the one adopted last year in Texas, where investors are now required to own at least $1 million in stock or a 3% stake to file a proposal with companies incorporated there.

Activist groups could still put out press releases saying that they want Exxon to pollute less or whatever, which would have roughly the same binding effect as putting it in Exxons proxy materials, but I guess putting it in the proxy materials has more symbolic oomph.

Tariff refunds are theoretically interesting because the importer who paid the tariff can sue to get its money back, but its not obvious that the economic incidence of the tariff is always on the importer. ... In a dissenting opinion, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh pointed out that the United States may be required to refund billions of dollars to importers who paid the IEEPA tariffs, even though some importers may have already passed on costs to consumers or others.  If you bought stuff on Amazon and Amazon gets a refund, can you ask for your cut?

title: Trump Asks Allies For Help With Hormuz, Nvidia GTC Underway | Bloomberg Businessweek Daily 3/16/2026
content: On today's episode of Bloomberg Businessweek Daily, Carol Massar and Tim Stenovec speak with Bloomberg Opinion international affairs columnist on President Trump's demands that allies back US efforts to protect tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and why some countries may want to use their assistance as leverage. Then, Alberto Gallo, CIO of Andromeda Capital Management, on the private credit landscape as investment in AI increases private credit funds' exposure to hyperscalers. Plus, Ed Ludlow breaks down what to expect from Nvidia's GTC conference - the super bowl of AI conferences - as the company tries to jumpstart the idling stock. Then, Racquel Oden, US head of international wealth and private banking at HSBC, talks market landscape as Wall Street tries to parse what's next in the war with Iran. (Source: Bloomberg)
